#3148. The Dynamo-Electric Principle: 160 Years of Powering Industry

How a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion helped shape the motors and generators that drive modern industry

Innomotics is a global leader in electric motors and large drive systems, operating from its headquarters in Nuremberg, Germany.

The dynamo-electric principle: one idea, 160 years, millions of motors.

This article is brought to you by Innomotics.

In the annals of industrial history, few innovations have demonstrated such remarkable staying power as the dynamo-electric principle. Discovered by Werner von Siemens in 1866, this groundbreaking principle remains fundamental to modern electrical engineering more than a century and a half later – and continues to shape the technology portfolio of Innomotics, a globally leading provider of electric motors and large drive systems. What began as a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion has evolved into a cornerstone of global industry – powering everything from brewery operations in Qingdao to high-voltage drive systems in petrochemical plants.

The year 1866 marked a decisive turning point, not only in the broader arc of industrial transformation but specifically in the realm of electric motion. At a time when Europe was entering a new phase of industrial transformation, Werner von Siemens pioneered the dynamo-electric principle – a breakthrough that enabled electric machines to generate their own magnetic field through self-excitation. This innovation transformed electric machines from laboratory curiosities into practical power sources, enabling the widespread electrification of industry and infrastructure that defined the late 19th century.

This electric motor from Innomotics was installed in the early 1900s at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China and supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions.Innomotics

The principle itself is elegantly simple: an iron core generates a stable magnetic field; a rotating coil is placed within this field; movement in the magnetic field induces an electric current; part of this current strengthens the magnetic field; and electrical energy is continuously converted into motion. This self-reinforcing cycle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

More than 160 years later, the same fundamental idea continues to power industrial applications around the world. Millions of motors operate reliably under demanding conditions, keeping production running across generations. The dynamo-electric principle made it possible for electric machines to convert electrical energy into motion (and motion back into electrical energy), creating the technological foundation for modern electric motors and drive systems.

Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) enhances stability and reliability by actively reducing vibrations.Innomotics

Perhaps no example illustrates this longevity better than the electric motor from Innomotics at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China. Installed in the early 1900s during the early electrification of industrial brewing, this motor supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions. It became a powerful example of long-term reliability in real-world applications – a testament to how engineering ensures reliable motion across decades.

Continuity, however, does not mean stagnation. Sixteen decades after the original breakthrough, innovations continue to emerge that build upon this proven foundation. Two recent developments – the Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) and oil-lubricated rolling bearings (OLRB) – carry this spirit of innovation and ingenuity forward, a commitment that has been recognized with the German Innovation Award.

Innomotics’ patented Oil-Lubricated Rolling Bearing (OLRB) technology enhances reliability and reduces maintenance requirements.Innomotics

AVCS helps optimize high-voltage motor performance by actively decoupling motors from their foundations to reduce vibration issues. OLRB helps prevent rolling bearing failures from the start with continuous lubrication, supporting higher availability, less downtime, and long-term cost savings. These innovations demonstrate how the basic principle of 1866 can be enhanced through modern engineering to meet contemporary demands for reliability and efficiency.

For three decades, with over 25,000 units driving performance globally, Innomotics’ Perfect Harmony GH180 medium-voltage drive platform has supported reliable operation across industries. Its modular architecture enables efficient power control, high availability, and long-term performance. With thousands of installations worldwide, Perfect Harmony GH180 continues to build on a proven technological foundation, minimizing downtime and ensuring stable production.

Keeping critical motors running requires the right expertise and innovation spirit throughout the entire lifecycle. With Innomotics Customer Services, operators and plant managers gain the insights they need to maintain reliability and optimize maintenance strategies. Winding Lifetime Analysis (WLA) combines operating history, machine measurements, and physics-based modeling to assess the condition of the winding insulation and estimate its remaining useful lifetime. This enables informed maintenance decisions, reduces uncertainty, and helps minimize the risk of unplanned downtime.

The Perfect Harmony GH180 delivers efficient, reliable and flexible medium-voltage drive performance.Innomotics

What began as a breakthrough in 1866 still brings its value to modern industry. The dynamo-electric principle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

As industries worldwide grapple with challenges ranging from energy efficiency to operational resilience, this 160-year-old principle continues to prove its relevance.

For plant managers and engineers seeking long-term performance in demanding applications, the message is clear: the foundation laid in the 19th century remains as solid as ever. What has changed are the tools and services built upon it – from vibration control systems to predictive analytics – all designed to extract maximum value from a principle that has, quite literally, powered the modern world for a century and a half.

Innomotics, carrying forward a legacy that spans the full arc of this history, continues to move industry forward with innovations that create real progress. The dynamo-electric principle may be 160 years old, but as the company’s portfolio demonstrates, it is far from obsolete. It is, in every sense of the word, still running.

Innomotics is a global leader in electric motors and large drive systems, operating from its headquarters in Nuremberg, Germany.

#3146. Apple HomeView review: An adorable smart display that earns its place

Apple’s HomeView smart display is here. It combines a 7-inch display with Siri AI and an all-new software experience that actually feels really familiar.

I’ve spent the last ten days living with HomeView in my kitchen. Here’s everything you need to know.

HomeView is an adorable little thing. That’s the best way to describe it. A 7-inch square display sits atop a rounded aluminum speaker base. A small, polished metal arm connects it and lets you tilt the display forward and backward.

HomeView comes in four colors: Starlight, Rose Pink, Silver, and Space Gray. My review unit is Starlight, and it’s very subtle. I had to double-check the box to make sure it was Starlight, not Silver.

The decision to make the display square is interesting. Between that design and the software experience centered around faces and widgets, HomeView really does feel like an oversized Apple Watch for your home.

I really appreciate the square display. It makes HomeView look less like an iPad propped up on a stand and more like a dedicated, purpose-driven device.

In terms of specs, the 7-inch display has a 1088 × 1088 resolution, equating to a pixel density of 220 pixels per inch. Max brightness is 500 nits. It can also dim all the way to 0.3 nits, which means it can go in a bedroom without being a nuisance. It also has True Tone to match your room’s lighting temperature.

For the past ten days, my partner and I have been living with HomeView on our kitchen counter. The square display and aluminum base look great in that setting. I don’t think an iPad-style display would look nearly as intentional. We also don’t have much spare counter space. If HomeView were any bigger or wider, I’m not sure we’d have room for it.

In the lead-up to HomeView’s launch, I was skeptical of how usable a 7-inch display would be. In practice, I’ve found this to be (mostly) a non-issue. Apple has done a great job optimizing the interface for the display. Text is readable at a glance from a few feet away, timers are nice and large, and the interface adapts to show more information when you’re closer.

Sometimes I wish it were bigger. Viewing a recipe requires a bit more scrolling than I would like. It’d be nice to fit a couple more widgets on the Modular face. But those trade-offs are easier to accept when I consider how much I appreciate HomeView’s compact footprint.

Apple touts that the HomeView has a custom-engineered acoustic system. There are two custom full-range drivers in the display, paired with a down-firing woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators in the base.

In practice, HomeView’s sound quality falls somewhere between the HomePod mini and the full-size second-generation HomePod. Its sound quality won’t blow you away, but it’s respectable for music and podcast playback. I replaced a full-size original HomePod in my kitchen with it, and while it doesn’t sound quite as good, it makes up for it in other ways … like by having a screen.

HomeView can serve as an AirPlay target, too, so you can beam content from your iPhone or other Apple device right to it. You can also AirPlay from HomeView to other AirPlay targets in your house.

HomeView doesn’t have any buttons, which is a design decision I’ve found very frustrating on multiple occasions. I wish it had volume buttons, so I could quickly adjust the volume without yelling at Siri or using the touchscreen.

HomeView’s software borrows heavily from iOS and watchOS. The interface is built around a system of faces with widgets, very similar to the Apple Watch’s complications system. The process of configuring a face will feel very familiar to Apple Watch and iPhone users.

You can customize faces by long-pressing on them, which reveals a familiar “Customize” screen. Here, you can change the style, color, widgets, and background. You can also add widgets from your nearby iPhone. Apple says that widgets are visible to everyone, but widget content is only visible while your primary device is in the home.

I’ve become particularly fond of the Modular face, which lets you place four equally sized square widgets. I think it provides a nice amount of glanceable information without feeling too dense. The Photos face is also a delight, essentially turning the HomeView into a digital picture frame. Support for Shared Albums is especially nice.

I think Apple made the right decision by building the HomeView experience around faces rather than a traditional app-focused interface. Most of the time, HomeView is just sitting on your counter or table, and you’re not actively interacting with it. That’s why I’ve gravitated towards the Modular face.

The faces system also means that HomeView doesn’t constantly draw your attention. Just like the physical design, it’s there when you need it, but otherwise does a good job blending into the background.

Swiping down from the left two-thirds of the display activates Siri AI, while swiping down from the top right takes you to Control Center (which annoyingly isn’t customizable). Swiping up from the bottom takes you to the Home Screen, where you’ll find a grid of apps and spots to add even more widgets.

There is no App Store on HomeView. Instead, there’s a collection of built-in Apple apps paired with audio and video apps through its CarPlay-based app system. Here are the Apple apps that are available on HomeView:

I’m hopeful that Apple builds on the app story for HomeView sooner rather than later. I don’t think HomeView needs its own App Store, but I do think it needs more apps. This includes more Apple apps and additional third-party apps.

I desperately want Apple to add the Notes app to HomeView. My wife and I keep recipes and dinner ideas in Notes, so it would be great to have that experience available on HomeView. It feels like an odd omission right now. HomeView also needs a dedicated Photos app.

I think the idea of basing the system on CarPlay makes sense. There are a lot of similarities in UI between how an app should work in the car and on a smart display. The Audible app, for example, translates really well from CarPlay to HomeView, as does Spotify.

However, the list of supported categories for CarPlay is a lot broader than the audio and video category Apple is allowing on HomeView right now. There are signs this could expand very soon, and I’m hopeful that’s the case.

One of the cleverest aspects of HomeView is its recipe experience. When you open a recipe in Safari, HomeView gives you the option to convert it into a dedicated cooking interface. You can browse for recipes directly on HomeView, or find one on your iPhone and simply hold it in front of HomeView to hand off the webpage.

HomeView then intelligently detects the actual recipe information and puts it into a streamlined interface. You can view the full ingredient list and measurements, and check off items as you go. The recipe itself is broken down into individual steps. It also intelligently identifies when you need to set a timer and gives you the option to start one directly from the recipe.

This is the exact type of feature that’s perfect for HomeView, and perfect for a dedicated screen sitting on the kitchen counter. You don’t have to keep reaching for your phone, unlocking it, and finding your place in the recipe.

The feature works incredibly well. I tried it with recipes of varying lengths from multiple different websites without any major problems.

There are some limitations, though. For example, it does struggle if a website splits the recipe into multiple pages. Also, as I mentioned earlier, the 7-inch display means there’s more scrolling involved than I’d like. It doesn’t solve my frustration with the lack of a dedicated Notes app. Still, it’s a great example of where this design excels.

Ultimately, the HomeView’s software interface is really well done. Delightful animations appear throughout the experience, like when notifications or the Siri blob slide in from the top bezel. Everything feels very smooth. The software feels familiar because of its similarities to Apple Watch and iPhone, but it’s also clearly purpose-built for the smart display form factor.

Since HomeView is meant for everyone in your home, Apple had to engineer a multi-user system. HomeView supports up to six people, each with their own personalized Home Screen, widgets, and access to personal information.

HomeView identifies the different people in your house in two ways: facial recognition and voice recognition. The goal is to recognize who’s interacting with it and customize the experience for that person. So, when I approach HomeView, it can recognize my face and display my calendar, reminders, and messages. When my wife approaches, it can recognize her instead and show her information.

The facial recognition implementation is particularly interesting. HomeView doesn’t have Face ID. Instead, it uses its built-in camera for facial recognition. During setup, you’re asked to turn your head left, right, up, and down so HomeView can capture your face from different angles.

In practice, HomeView’s facial recognition works surprisingly well. I was skeptical, but it’s done a good job of identifying both my wife and me. If I approach it and try to open the Messages app while it’s on my wife’s profile, I get a message saying it can’t verify my identity. If I repeatedly try, HomeView disables facial recognition, requiring my wife to authenticate using her iPhone before she can access her personal information again.

In addition to protecting personal data, HomeView does a decent job of automatically switching between profiles. There’s occasionally a delay of a few seconds, so I wish it were slightly faster.

HomeView is powered by Apple’s A18 chip, which enables support for Siri AI. However, Siri AI works a bit differently on HomeView than on other Apple devices.

HomeView can answer world knowledge questions on its own, without relying on a paired iPhone or iPad. This is basically the trivia questions we’ve all grown accustomed to shouting at voice assistants over the years. The difference, of course, is that Siri AI answers these questions well, unlike old Siri. On HomeView, the experience is even better because you can visually see the response on the display, often accompanied by images or other visual information.

The second aspect of Siri AI is personal context. To use Siri AI’s personal context on HomeView, you need an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad in your house.

Apple says that the device must have been recently unlocked and be connected to the same Wi-Fi network as HomeView.

In my testing over the last 10 days, I’ve never run into a situation where HomeView was unable to answer a Siri AI query because my iPhone was unavailable.

I’ve found Siri AI to be quite impressive and useful since it debuted in September. It’s a huge upgrade over old Siri. Broadly speaking, that experience extends to HomeView.

Many of the same personal context questions I ask on my iPhone can now be answered by HomeView. And because of HomeView’s form factor, it’s more useful when multitasking. Instead of reaching for my iPhone or hoping it’s within earshot, I can just ask HomeView.

Here are a few questions HomeView has answered without a hiccup:

In terms of speed, I’ve found HomeView to be slightly slower to answer personal context questions than my iPhone Duo. It’s not a huge difference, but it’s a few seconds each time. I assume this is because HomeView is basically handing off the request to my iPhone, adding an additional step that requests directly on the iPhone don’t have to do.

Siri AI is not without its faults. There are times on HomeView where it just hangs and never responds, or responds with a generic “Sorry, try again later” message of some sort. HomeView’s primary interaction method is your voice, which makes these types of Siri AI failures even more frustrating.

HomeView can also serve as the command center for your smart home. It has a dedicated Home app, as well as multiple different Home-focused face options. You can also, of course, use your voice to control HomeKit accessories and scenes through Siri.

There’s ultimately nothing particularly remarkable about HomeView’s support for smart home control. It offers much of the same functionality as the Home app on your iPhone, but in one central location that everyone in your house can use.

There is one limitation: you currently can’t use Siri AI on HomeView to control secure devices like locks and garage doors, even if the device recognizes you. If they are part of a scene, you can tell Siri AI to set the scene and it works. But you can’t individually control them.

Apple tells Joanna Stern that a software update coming next month will add security accessory support to HomeView’s Siri AI.

I wish Apple would expand what HomeView can do for the smart home. It has a built-in camera, so why can’t I use that camera for motion sensing or as a HomeKit Secure Video camera?

I’ve found the screen most useful for quickly checking the status of accessories, like seeing whether a door is locked or glancing at the doorbell camera. For actually controlling accessories, I still find Siri and automations to be the easiest approach. HomeView hasn’t really changed that, although I do appreciate being able to adjust the thermostat right from the kitchen counter.

HomeView costs $299, which is about $100 less than I expected based on rumors. That’s a surprisingly reasonable price, I think. The key, of course, is whether you’ll actually use it day to day.

When you get a new iPhone, you already have a pretty good idea of what you’ll use it for and where it fits into your life. New features might change how you use it, but the core functionality stays the same.

HomeView is very different. At first, it sits on your counter and is nice to look at. It’s a very, very cute little thing. But it takes time to discover how and why it fits into your life.

At first, I had no idea whether I’d actually use HomeView. But in the ten days it’s been sitting on my counter, it’s grown on me quite a bit. It’s gone from being a nice-to-have to something I use and rely on for multiple tasks each day.

It’s also been interesting watching my partner interact with it. Her first impression was essentially, “It’s cute, but I don’t know what I’ll use it for.” Over the last week, however, she’s remarked multiple times how much she likes it.

Whether it’s personal context-focused Siri AI interactions, simply being able to glance and see how long is left on a timer, watching the animated album art as a song plays, or the joy of the Photos face, HomeView has earned its spot.

In fact, I moved HomeView from our kitchen to my office for a day to test a few features and settings in more depth. While cooking dinner that night, we both found ourselves shouting Siri commands into the air and glancing at the empty spot on the counter, only to remember it wasn’t there.

I think that’s the best example of what makes HomeView special. You don’t have to be a HomeKit enthusiast or spend hours tinkering with smart home automations to appreciate it. It’s a device everyone in the house can find their own uses for, and it becomes more useful the longer it’s part of your routine.

Ice storms cause long outages because several exposures act together. Ice adds weight to conductors, hardware and structures. Wind pushes on the larger iced surface. Trees and limbs bend into the line and add impact and uneven load. Conductors may also gallop and lose clearance. This paper explains how these loads combine and why the complete line must be assessed, not a single component. It reviews a monitored winter test of three conductor systems. It also summarizes utility records from a major regional ice storm. Finally, it outlines how to choose corridors, plan restoration and keep crews and the public safe around covered conductors.

#3144. Google’s new Android XR glasses work with iOS, Made for iPhone certified

Google today announced Android XR audio glasses called Intelligent Eyewear that notably support iOS with Made for iPhone certification.

Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20

Intelligent Eyewear is made by Samsung with frame designs from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker. There are 30 unique designs in total, and the frames weigh 40-44 grams with a 12-megapixel ultra-wide camera.

Google’s Glasses companion client for iOS handles compute, including HDR processing, and saves images and videos (up to 90 seconds) to Apple Photos. The Made for iPhone certification comes into play for Wi-Fi Aware connectivity that allows for fast media transfers.

Gemini commands that use the camera, like visual search or translation, don’t trigger the light because those photos or videos are not saved anywhere, including Gemini History. Before that media reaches the cloud, Google redacts faces from video feeds and filters out bystander voices. This processing is done by the companion app. Additionally, that media isn’t used to train AI models or target ads.

Other key specifications include four microphones and two open-ear speakers. Besides voice commands with the “Hey Gemini” hotword, there is a touchpad that accepts taps and swipes. A physical on/off switch lets you wear Intelligent Eyewear as regular glasses.

On iOS, Gemini can make calls, send 1:1 messages (including via iMessage), and receive notifications.

Battery life is rated at nine hours on a single charge, while there’s a charging case that stores seven charges. Features include turn-by-turn Google Maps directions and real-time translation. On the streaming front, there’s support for Apple Music, Spotify, YouTube Music, and Audible.

Google’s Android XR glasses require an iPhone 13 Pro or newer.

Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear is available in three frame designs, starting at $395 for optical and sun styles. Gentle Monster Intelligent Eyewear is available in the US and South Korea from $449.

Pre-orders open today with retail availability on December 10.

Led by a gun-toting Keira Knightley, "Black Doves" was a hit for Netflix pretty much straight out of the nest: When the spy thriller premiered on the streaming service in late 2024, it quickly reached No. 1 on Netflix's global charts and accumulated 10.8 million views during its opening week. So it wasn't a surprise that the streamer greenlit "Black Doves" season 2, nor that the new eps—which hit the platform on November 5—have reached No. 2 on Netflix's weekly TV charts.

The second season sees Knightley's Helen Webb balance her clandestine career as an undercover spy with her husband Wallace's (Andrew Buchan) new role as the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. Meanwhile, Helen's old pal Sam (Ben Whishaw) is blackmailed by Patrick (Sam Riley), an operative working for a rival underground organization.

It's plenty of drama for a six-episode run, so we wouldn't blame you if you've already sped through the recent season. If you're still after some more action-packed thrillers, political dramas, and the like, however, here are three shows to check out after you've finished "Black Doves" season 2.

Like the Knightley-led "Black Doves," this Apple TV spy thriller stars another British acting icon, Gary Oldman: The Oscar winner plays Jackson Lamb, the foul-mouthed, chain-smoking head of Slough House, a sort of administrative purgatory for spies who’ve made career-ending mistakes. (That disgraced team includes the illustrious likes of Kristin Scott Thomas, Jonathan Pryce, Jack Lowden and Olivia Cooke.)

”Slow Horses” recently wrapped up its six-episode sixth season (which Tom’s Guide’s own Malcolm McMillan called one of the 10 best shows of 2026 so far) and has already been picked up for a seventh and eighth installment, so if you haven’t yet checked out the Emmy-winning thriller, a post-“Black Doves” binge is a great move.

Oscar winner Eddie Redmayne stars as the titular Jackal, an elite, anonymous assassin hired to take out tech billionaire Ulle Dag Charles (Khalid Abdalla), in this 10-episode espionage thriller. However, that lucrative gig—which sees him having to deploy theatrical disguises, multiple languages and lethal marksmanship—gets exponentially harder when the hired gun starts being hunted by a tenacious British intelligence officer (Lashana Lynch), kicking off a high-stakes cat-and-mouse chase across Europe.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

”The Day of the Jackal” season one was a hit with critics (it has an 85% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, with the pros praising Redmayne's “reptilian” performance in particular) and viewers alike (the spy show became Peacock's most-watched new original drama series after its first 75 days on the platform). A second season is officially scheduled to premiere in spring 2027 on Peacock in the U.S. and Sky in the U.K., with new cast members Matt Bomer, Weruche Opia, and Pablo Schreiber joining the undercover fun.

Stream "The Day of the Jackal" on Peacock now

Season two of “Black Doves” sees Knightley’s character balancing her career as a lethal spy with her role as the Prime Minister’s wife at 10 Downing Street. There’s a similar tension to be found in Netflix’s “The Diplomat,” where Keri Russell’s strong-willed and sharp-minded Kate Wyler must juggle her professional ambitions as the U.S. Ambassador to the U.K. with her personal duties to her husband Hal (Rufus Sewell), who, by the fourth season of the political drama, ascends to the Vice Presidency of the United States.

There might not be “Black Doves”-style spy antics in “The Diplomat,” but the fast-paced series is packed with political subterfuge, back-channel backstabbing and international intrigue. Tom’s Guide’s Kelly Woo praised the show’s most recent edition as “its best season yet”: “Season 4 doubles down on what has always made the show so much fun: putting brilliant, deeply complicated people in rooms together and watching them try to outmaneuver one another while barely holding their personal lives together,” writes Woo.

#3142. Apple Home Collection accessories available for pre-order this Friday

Apple’s new HomeView (review here) and Apple TV 4K (review) arrive in stores this Friday, November 13. And that same day, the first Apple Home Collection accessories will be available for pre-order.

If you’re looking to upgrade your smart home, Apple will soon have a lot of new options for you.

The HomeView and new Apple TV 4K launch this Friday, November 13. We’ve just published our HomeView review and Apple TV 4K review.

Joining these products, Apple has worked closely with LG and Schneider to develop a suite of smart home accessories announced as part of a new ‘Apple Home Collection.’

These accessories include smart thermostats, security cameras, video doorbells, and more.

The first Apple Home Collection products will launch in December. And now Apple has confirmed to 9to5Mac that pre-orders for select accessories will open this Friday, November 13 on Apple.com.

Apple hasn’t yet said which accessories will be part of this initial batch, but we’ll keep you posted as more information emerges.

The pitch for Apple Home Collection products is that Apple co-developed them, and they’re designed to offer easy setup in the Home app with no third-party apps or accounts required. The accessories also take advantage of the latest Apple Home technologies, such as Adaptive Temperature for smart thermostats.

Scarlet Witch might have one of the most interesting roles to play in “Avengers: Doomsday,” and I’m not just saying that because Wanda Maximoff is one of my favorite Marvel characters. After seemingly meeting her end in “Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness,” fans have been waiting to find out whether Elizabeth Olsen will return to the MCU. Now, with Doctor Doom seemingly taking an interest in Wanda and her extraordinary powers, there’s plenty of room for speculation about what Marvel has planned.

But why would Doom need Scarlet Witch in the first place? Wanda is one of the most powerful magic users in the Marvel universe, with reality-altering abilities that could make her an incredibly valuable ally or a terrifying enemy. Her comic-book history also offers some intriguing possibilities, particularly when you look at storylines like “House of M” and “The Children’s Crusade.”

Of course, Marvel hasn’t confirmed exactly how Wanda fits into “Avengers: Doomsday,” so we’ll have to wait and see how much of this speculation holds up. Still, there are several fascinating directions the studio could take her story. Here are five Scarlet Witch theories that could explain Doctor Doom’s interest in Wanda and what her potential MCU comeback might look like.

One popular theory is that “Avengers: Doomsday” could take inspiration from Marvel Comics’ “The Children’s Crusade.” In the comic, Wanda disappears after the events of “Avengers Disassembled” and “House of M.” Her sons, Billy and Tommy, eventually set out to find her with the Young Avengers. They discover that Wanda is living in Latveria with Doctor Doom, having lost her memories. Doom is secretly using her powerful magic for his own purposes. The young heroes eventually confront him and help Wanda escape, revealing that she has been manipulated rather than acting as a villain herself.

There are a few reasons this storyline could work in the MCU. At the end of “VisionQuest,” Vision, Billy and Tommy are together, leaving Wanda as the missing member of the family. One possibility is that Doom could erase Wanda’s memories or take advantage of her vulnerability to control her powers.

He might even use her desire to reunite with her family to keep her on his side. Of course, Marvel hasn't confirmed that it’s adapting this storyline, and we don’t yet know how much of the comic could make it into the movie. It’s also possible that Wanda’s reunion with her children will be saved for “Avengers: Secret Wars” instead.

Scarlet Witch could be connected to a mysterious group of masked characters known as the “Latverian Witches.” These figures have appeared in “Avengers: Doomsday” promotional material, including posters, convention displays and leaked concept art. One particular poster caught fans’ attention because one of the masked witches is red. This has led to speculation that Scarlet Witch could be part of the group, possibly working alongside Doctor Doom.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

There have also been reports of a “Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness” page on Disney+ featuring promotional artwork showing Wanda and Doctor Strange in front of a Latverian mural. However, the details surrounding the witches are still unclear. Some reports describe three masked figures wearing different colored robes, while others point to artwork featuring four characters. There is no official confirmation that Wanda is one of them.

This theory also fits with the idea that Doom is gathering powerful characters to help carry out his plans. In the post-credits scene attached to the “Avengers: Endgame” theatrical rerelease, Doom approaches Bruce Banner in an underground bunker and tells him, “I've come to collect you.” Banner then disappears alongside Doom, leaving behind a glowing green symbol. We know he’s also collected Scarlet Witch, meaning these “witches” might all hold a special power to help Doom complete his plans.

It’s possible that Scarlet Witch could take the place of Molecule Man in Marvel’s “Secret Wars” storyline. In the comics, Doctor Doom uses enormous amounts of power to reshape reality and create Battleworld, a world made from the remains of destroyed universes. He then rules over it as God Emperor Doom.

Some fans think Marvel could use Wanda instead of introducing Molecule Man, especially since she’s already an established character with incredible reality-warping abilities. We’ve seen her create an entire town in “WandaVision” and travel between universes in “Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness.” That makes her a believable target for Doom, particularly after his apparent promise that her power will be his.

But how would he use it? One possibility is that Doom steals Wanda’s chaos magic to build Battleworld and take control of the multiverse. This could also connect to the Darkhold prophecy mentioned in “Agatha All Along,” which claims that the Scarlet Witch is destined to destroy the world.

There’s another possibility, though. Rather than simply forcing Wanda to help him, Doom could offer her a deal. He might promise to create a new reality where she can live happily with Vision, Billy and Tommy in exchange for her help. That would give Wanda a personal reason to side with him, even if she doesn’t fully understand his plans. It could also set up a heartbreaking conflict when her family discovers what Doom has done.

One of the biggest theories following “VisionQuest” is that Doctor Doom could use Wanda to destroy Earth-10005, the universe home to the original Fox “X-Men” movies. “Avengers: Doomsday” is expected to bring together heroes from three different universes: the MCU’s Earth-616, the Fantastic Four’s Earth-828 and the X-Men’s Earth-10005. With Marvel planning to introduce its own version of the X-Men after this saga, some fans believe the Fox universe could be destroyed as part of the story.

This theory has an interesting connection to House of M, one of Scarlet Witch’s most famous comic-book storylines. In it, Wanda utters the iconic line “No more mutants,” causing mutants to lose their powers. Elizabeth Olsen has previously said she would love to deliver the line in the MCU, but there’s been no opportunity yet. Having Wanda use her powers against the Fox “X-Men” universe could be Marvel’s way of bringing that moment to life.

It’s possible that the Sentinels shown in the “Doomsday” trailer might actually be designed to contain Wanda rather than hunt mutants. There’s also a less villainous possibility. Instead of Wanda destroying the mutants, she could turn against Doom and use her powers to stop him from wiping them out. This could lead to a twist on her famous comic-book line: “No, more mutants.” It might even set up the arrival of mutants in the rebooted MCU.

As we know in the “VisionQuest” finale, the post-credit scene revisits Wanda’s apparent death beneath Mount Wundagore in “Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness,” but this time we see what happened after the temple collapsed. Doctor Doom uses green magic to lift the rubble before telling Wanda, “Scarlet Witch, awaken. Your power will be mine.” Moments later, her eyes open.

But how exactly did Doom bring her back? One popular fan theory says Wanda never actually died. Instead, the red flash of magic seen as Wundagore collapsed could have been her Chaos Magic protecting her and placing her in some kind of healing coma. Doom may simply have found her and awakened her. Another possibility is that Doom rescued Wanda immediately after the collapse but kept her hidden for years. This would explain why nobody else managed to find her and why she was considered gone. Some fans even believe he could have used time travel to return to the moment Wundagore fell and save her.

There’s also the possibility that Wanda really did die and Doom used magic to resurrect her. In fact, he could have stolen power from Franklin Richards, who demonstrated the ability to bring someone back to life in “The Fantastic Four: First Steps.” Whatever the explanation, Doom clearly has a reason for bringing Wanda back, and his warning that her power will be his suggests she’s central to his plans, and could be the most powerful weapon against the Avengers.

Alix is a Senior Streaming Writer at Tom’s Guide, which basically means watching the best movies and TV shows and then writing about them. It’s a dream job for someone who’s been obsessed with storytelling since she first figured out how to work a remote.

She heads to the cinema every week as a tradition, no matter what’s showing. For her, movies aren’t just entertainment — they’re a ritual, a comfort, and a constant source of inspiration. When she’s not at her desk or at the cinema, you’ll probably find her deep into a horror video game on her PC.

You can ditch a few other devices if you pick up an iPhone Duo

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Do you remember that controversial iPad Pro advert a couple of years back? The one where a hydraulic press crushed the piano, the painting, the arcade cabinet and a bunch of other stuff into Apple’s super-slim premium tablet? It didn’t go down well at the time, but it’s crept into my mind a couple of times after having used the iPhone Duo as my daily driver for the last couple of weeks.

That’s because Apple’s foldable phone does such a good job of being a flexible everyday tool that it’s replaced a bunch of single-use items I carry in a typical day.

Then again, I'd expect nothing less from a device with a starting price of $2,000. And we can debate the benefits of dedicated devices vs. all-rounders, but the Duo has a couple of things going for it that some of the other best foldable phones may have struggled with.

For example, the software continuity is seriously impressive when you unfold because of the matched aspect ratio between the screens and the fact iOS 27 doesn’t restart whatever application you’re using when you switch. Therefore, app state, scroll position and active text entry remain completely consistent when you switch from the 5.4-inch closed screen to the 7.6-inch open display.

On top of that, the nano-texture coating on the interior screen makes a huge difference when it comes to reading and, eventually, writing. Especially if you plan to use the Duo outside. There’s very little reflective glare and the IP68 waterproofing means you don’t need to worry about getting it out in the rain.

So, let's dig into the five things I’ve (mostly) been able to ditch after going all-in on the Duo

I’m starting this list off with something of an asterisk. Because, although the iPhone Duo now supports stylus input through iOS 27.2, only one Apple Pencil is actually compatible. That’s the Apple Pencil (USB-C) and not, frustratingly, the Apple Pencil 2nd Gen that I use with my iPad. It’ll set you back $79 if you do decide to pick one up, and I’m still weighing up whether or not to splash the cash. I’ll be keeping an eye on the Black Friday sales for that one.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

Either way, a notebook and pen or pencil have been a staple of my day job for years. But unlike the Duo, my paper notebook won’t fold easily and it’ll stop working if it gets wet. Also, thanks to the Duo’s nano-texture display, you get a little bit more friction that feels more like writing on actual paper. The Duo will let you write in Notes, sketch in Freeform and, crucially, mark up screenshots and documents for easy sharing.

I’m still rocking the original Nintendo Switch as my portable game console of choice and despite the excellent back catalog, it’s starting to show its age.

The Switch 1’s 6.2-inch, 60Hz display only boasts a 720p resolution and, obviously, doesn’t fold. So while it is a handheld, it can’t hold a candle to the iPhone Duo’s 7.6-inch Super Retina XDR OLED screen with a 120Hz refresh rate and 1878 x 2670 resolution. And if you’ve got an AirPlay-enabled TV you can mirror Duo games to your bigger screen Switch-style and play with a Bluetooth controller.

Apple’s own catalog is nowhere close to Nintendo, but performance is streets ahead thanks to the A20 Pro chip. The Duo can handle AAA games like the Resident Evil, Civilization VII and GRID series no problem. There are some fun Duo-optimised games like Battleship Duo that take advantage of the form factor.

My one complaint is that while the Netflix app has been adapted to the Duo, that doesn’t extend to the games. Which is a bummer as I’ve recently started out on the original Red Dead Redemption after finding it on Netlfix’s mobile game library.

This one is a bit of a sliding scale, depending on the size, but I usually have a paperback with me for the commute. My colleagues Nick and Anthony both recommend the Xteink X4 e-reader as a more portable option, but the Duo nails this use case completely.

Apple Books is a joy to use on the nano-texture display, and the page-turning animation is both smooth and satisfying. You can even set up a Duo-specific shortcut that opens Books automatically when you unfold to minimize distractions and get straight to reading time.

Even with the Duo in my pocket, I likely won’t give up paperback books altogether. Magazines are a different story, though. On the Duo, you can appreciate the visual element of a magazine and still pinch to zoom in to make that text a little easier to read. You can also screenshot and annotate certain parts to read later — great for a recipe or workout.

I’m a huge fan of magazines (Future Publishing, Tom’s Guide’s parent company, produces dozens of beautiful magazines every month), and being able to fold literally dozens away in my pocket is a trick I’ll never stop appreciating.

This is probably a bit obvious, but given the points above and the entire sentiment of this article, I’ve always liked smaller tablets. They sit right in that sweet spot between the laptop and the smartphone to give you a more immersive experience for reading and watching without taking up valuable bag space. I’ve had the Xiaomi Pad Mini for about a year and, after seeing the pricing for the new iPad mini 8, I’ll likely be using it a bit longer.

Except for the fact that the iPhone Duo completely overshadows small tablets for me. Since Apple’s folding phone arrived in my hands, it really has become the iPad mini alternative I’ve always wanted.

The iPhone Duo isn’t the first foldable I’ve used with regularity, but it’s the first one that genuinely feels like it can replace the dedicated devices I’ve used for years. Power and durability are one thing, but Apple’s decision to implement the matte, nano-texture coating on the interior screen is another big reason why — it’s honestly a game-changer for reading and writing. And there could have been a few other items on this list, like a bedside alarm clock or a camera tripod, without too much trouble.

What blows my mind is that, right now, the iPhone Duo is the worst it’s ever going to be. Apple will refine and improve the product with future iterations at the same time as developers optimize their apps (and bring out new ones) to let you use the Duo for even more tasks. No hydraulic press necessary.

There’s no shortage of note-taking apps on the App Store, but Apple Notes has long been my favorite, and in iOS 27.3 it’s gaining a new advantage: extensive app controls via Siri AI.

Voice-driven computing is on the rise, with AI assistants—including Siri AI—now more capable and intelligent than ever.

Siri AI is already a big upgrade over the old Siri, but it’s getting even better in iOS 27.3.

As we reported last week, iOS 27.3 gives Siri AI many new capabilities across built-in Apple apps on your iPhone, iPad, Mac, and more.

The one I’ve been testing the most is Apple Notes. Siri has offered basic Notes-related functionality for years, but it gains a whole new set of powers with the new update.

Here’s everything Siri told me it can do in Notes as of iOS 27.3:

That’s a lot of capabilities that can all now be handled by Siri.

I have nearly 3,000 notes saved in Apple Notes and use the app every day, so it’s been fun seeing what Siri can now do for me. These Netflix movies actually deserved to wear the No. 1 crown

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I track the Netflix top 10 movies chart daily, and if there’s one thing I’ve learned, it’s that just because a movie claims the No. 1 spot doesn’t guarantee it’s good. Skipable movies seem to secure the honor frequently.

Per Netflix’s own tracking website, 30 movies have ranked No. 1 on Netflix U.S. so far this year, and I’ve combed through the data to find the five movies actually worth watching. Cards on the table, this was surprisingly tough; not due to an abundance of excellent options, but the opposite. A lot of subpar flicks have scored a No. 1 in 2026 (so far). Far too many, in fact.

Still, I’ve been able to bring together a fivesome of generally solid Netflix movies, featuring huge stars like Matt Damon, Ben Affleck, Paul Rudd, Melanie Lynskey, Jake Gyllenhaal and more. These are the Netflix No. 1 movies deserving of your time. And I've also added the full list below.

“The Rip” debuted on Netflix back in mid-January, and all these months later I still rank it as the streamer’s best original movie of 2026. It’s not that “The Rip” is some flawless masterpiece either. Instead, it’s merely an engaging action-thriller with a solid cast. The fact it’s still my favorite Netflix No. 1 of the year speaks to the overall poor quality of Netflix’s original movie slate lately. But at least “The Rip” remains a rare Netflix movie that didn’t disappoint.

Teaming up longtime friends and collaborators Ben Affleck and Matt Damon, “The Rip” centers on a group of Miami cops who stumble upon a $20 million stash during a house search. Unsure whose money they've just found, the police unit faces potential criminal retaliation, not to mention evaporating trust as each member of the team suspects the others might be looking to steal the money for themselves. It’s simple action-thriller fun.

“Anaconda” was one of 2025’s most overlooked movies, so I was pleased to see it get a second chance in the spotlight when it was added to Netflix’s library earlier this year. This could have been a creatively bankrupt remake of the 1997 cult comedy-horror, but it’s anything but a cheap cash-in. Instead, it opts for a fresh meta-twist that smartly comments on the nature of Hollywood reboots, while celebrating the fan-favorite original.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Childhood friends Doug (Jack Black) and Griff (Paul Rudd) are two middle-aged men who never managed to achieve their dreams. Fed up with the daily grind of their unsatisfying lives, they decide to head to the Amazon Rainforest to film an ultra-low-budget remake of their favorite movie of all time — you’ve guessed it, “Anaconda.” Once on location, friendships are tested, and the situation becomes too real when a giant snake attacks.

Sophie Birenbaum (Sandler) is over the moon when she lands the lead role in her high school’s production of “Waitress.” But while she deals with stage anxiety, being cast opposite her crush (Jack Champion) and perfecting a Southern accent, mom Elizabeth (Lynskey) is battling for her life against a serious illness. It’s a mother-daughter story with a big heart, and it swerves some of the worst genre impulses by largely avoiding cheap melodrama.

Watch "Don't Say Good Luck" on Netflix now

Another Ben Affleck movie on this list, “Animals,” is a considerable step below “The Rip,” and in a year with better options probably wouldn’t make the cut. But as noted, 2026 has been a weak year for Netflix, which sees it sneak into my list. “Animals” does have its moment of enthralling tension, and Gillian Anderson is excellent in a supporting role. Nevertheless, the biggest crime is ending on a very sour note thanks to a finale that skips straight over slightly silly and finds itself in absolutely ludicrous territory.

Affleck plays Mark Kimball, an L.A. mayoral candidate who has poured all his family’s money into his campaign, neglecting to tell his wife (Kerry Washington) about the financial gamble. When his son is kidnapped and those responsible demand an eye-watering ransom, Kimball and his wife Abigail must turn to a fixer (Anderson) to resolve the matter. “Animals” shows potential at first, but never fully sings, and the ending is especially awful.

Netflix's latest original movies tend to hold the No. 1 spot. Unsurprising, as these are the flicks the streaming service pushes most aggressively via its recommendation algorithm. However, occasionally a library title (aka a movie not produced or distributed by Netflix) will manage to hold the top spot. A recent example was 2004 disaster movie “The Day After Tomorrow," a big-budget blockbuster from Roland Emmerich, director of “Independence Day.”

To set expectations, “The Day After Tomorrow” does have its flaws, namely a corny screenplay, but its effects are impressive, particularly by mid-2000s standards, and the scenes of cities like New York City getting decimated by extreme weather are impactful. The movie stars Dennis Quaid, Jake Gyllenhaal and Ian Holm. Consider this one a pulpy guilty pleasure, and I’ll admit to having a nostalgic bias as I saw this film in my formative years.

Watch "The Day After Tomorrow" on Netflix now

#3134. Pedro sulla Lazio di Gattuso: «La città e i tifosi della Lazio meritano»

Lo spagnolo si augura che la squadra conservi il rendimento attuale; sul ritiro racconta le difficoltà di recupero.

Pedro è felice per la Lazio prima in classifica e riconosce l’impatto di Gennaro Gattuso sulla squadra. Intervistato da Cadena SER nel programma El Larguero, l’ex biancoceleste ha parlato del gioco dei suoi vecchi compagni e della decisione di chiudere la carriera al termine della scorsa stagione.

CLICCA QUI E SEGUI LAZIOPRESS.IT ANCHE SU INSTAGRAM

Pedro ha raccontato come è maturata la decisione: «Inizialmente pensavo di aspettare ancora un po’ per capire se sarebbe arrivata qualche possibilità di continuare, ma con il tempo ho capito quanto mi facesse stare bene avere più spazio per la famiglia e gli amici». Sul piano fisico, ha aggiunto: «Ho scelto in base alle sensazioni fisiche: nell’ultima stagione recuperare dopo le partite e ritrovare il ritmo era diventato sempre più complicato».

Pedro ne ha parlato con le persone a lui più vicine e ha maturato la scelta senza viverla come una conseguenza di un malessere: «A un certo punto della carriera bisogna ascoltare questi segnali. Ne ho parlato con le persone più vicine e ho deciso con serenità, perché non stavo male: semplicemente ho ritenuto fosse arrivato il momento giusto».

Guardando alla posizione occupata oggi dalla Lazio, Pedro ha scherzato sulla propria assenza: «Vedere la Lazio prima senza di me mi fa pensare che forse avrei dovuto partire prima… oppure restare un’altra stagione!». Poi ha chiarito il senso delle sue parole: «Scherzi a parte, sono davvero felice per loro. Si vede quanto abbia inciso Gattuso e sento parlare molto bene del suo lavoro».

I put these two top-tier watches to the test in the water

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Garmin Fenix 9 Pro are both top-of-the-range watches, with all the sports modes and stats you could need to track workouts. I’ve been testing both since they launched earlier this year, and I ran a marathon with both watches on my wrist a few weeks ago.

Next up, I wanted to see how both watches performed in the water. To find out, I strapped a watch to one wrist and used my Speedo iQ Vanquisher 3.0 goggles to measure how far I swam and how fast. When I got back on dry land, I downloaded all the data to see which watch came out on top — read on to find out more.

Let’s start with how these trackers measure your swimming workouts. Both use an internal accelerometer and gyroscope to recognise arm pulls and calculate how many strokes you take per length, as well as your stroke rate (strokes per minute). Both watches are waterproof to 10m, do automatic stroke detection, and can give you a SWOLF score — a measurement of stroke efficiency.

There’s a slight difference in usability between the two watches in the pool, namely down to the watch design. The Garmin Fenix 9 Pro has five leakproof buttons — three on the left, two on the right — which make navigating the watch in the pool a dream. The Apple Watch Ultra 4, on the other hand, locks the screen when you’re in the pool, so you’re relying on the Action Button to pause your workout, but you’ll have to deactivate the Water Lock to stop your swim.

As a control, I used my Speedo iQ Vanquisher 3.0 goggles. These smart goggles give you a wealth of data when you’re back on dry land. As well as your pace, distance, and how long you spent resting at the side of the pool, you can also see your head position, breath time and distance per stroke for each stroke.

I recently did this same test with the Apple Watch Series 12 and Fitbit Edge, and the Apple Watch won. Looking at the data, the same is true for the Apple Watch Ultra 4, which was, once again, spot on during this swim.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The Garmin Fenix 9 Pro recorded an extra 40m, which is only two lengths of the 20m pool I was swimming in, so it’s not in any way inaccurate, but just not quite as close as the Apple Watch Ultra 4.

Looking at the stroke breakdown in the Garmin Connect app, the Fenix 9 Pro also seemed to randomly mix up strokes, finding it harder to differentiate between freestyle and breaststroke. This led the watch to largely record my swim as "Mixed," rather than giving me a proper breakdown of each stroke.

Again, there’s not an awful lot in this, but it’s worth highlighting how accurately the Apple Watch Ultra 4 performed here. In the water, I definitely found the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro easier to use, plus you can connect the Fenix 9 Pro with a compatible HRM Swim chest strap, whereas you can’t do the same on the Apple Watch.

I’ll continue testing both watches, so stay tuned, but which would you pick between the two? Let us know in the poll below:

#3131. Google announces Gemini 4 Hydrogen with ‘significant leaps’ in speed, intelligence

After this week’s Carbon availability, Google today unveiled Gemini 4 Hydrogen instead of keeping the “Flash” branding. This model is billed as bringing “cutting-edge intelligence to everyone.”

Compared to Gemini 3.8 Flash (which launched in September), Hydrogen is billed as a “major standalone upgrade” with “significant leaps in both speed and intelligence.” It offers native 1 million-token input and up to 1 million output tokens. Specifically:

“Hydrogen surpasses Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level (51 vs. 50, and reaching 54 at its highest xhigh thinking setting), while often completing tasks faster than models in its class.”

In the Gemini app, Hydrogen is better at following and sticking to your tone, format, and rules, while offering clear tables and visual breakdowns. As such, “email drafts, study guides, rewrites, and documents come back ready to use on the first try.” Additionally, Hydrogen “more frequently calls the right tools (i.e., Connected Apps) and skills for the job.”

In the model picker, 4 Hydrogen is billed as providing “Everyday help.”

Free users in the Gemini app get access to Hydrogen via the “[Auto] model selection when it’s the appropriate model for the prompt.”

Google says Hydrogen significantly upgrades Search (AI Mode) by better understanding your intent:

…you can ask your question in your natural flow of thought — even if you have multiple parts to your query, hard-to-understand typos, or highly specific requests — and Search will intelligently comprehend what you’re looking for.

Responses get more visual and will feature a wider range of relevant links. Hydrogen is the default model for AI Mode and is used for “your hardest questions” in AI Overviews.

This was a nice surprise when I opened the app an hour or two ago. It seems to be noticeably better, too.

In Google Antigravity, 4 Hydrogen has an “Extra” thinking tier alongside Low, Medium, and High. Then there’s Orchestrator: “Carbon that may offload routine steps to Hydrogen. Same Carbon-level quality, fewer tokens used.”

To help make this multi-model collaboration automatic, we’re introducing Orchestrator in Google Antigravity. Rather than using a single model from start to finish, Orchestrator dynamically switches between models like Carbon and Hydrogen within the same session.

For workflows that require parallel agents, Carbon can act as the coordinator while Hydrogen can power worker and verifier agents to build and test changes simultaneously across isolated workspaces — helping teams ship complex projects faster without driving up token costs.

For developers, Hydrogen costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens.

What we know about the next generation of Samsung's flagship

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Samsung is mixing things up by offering a fourth version of the Samsung Galaxy S27. But this isn't another super-skinny Edge; it's the Samsung Galaxy S27 Pro. This phone is expected to sit between the Plus and Ultra models, offering more premium features than a Plus, but at a slightly lower price tag than the Ultra.

Obviously this is a brand new kind of phone, so it's not like we can look back at previous generations to guess at what might be coming. This makes the S27 Pro a lot more mysterious than the rest of the S27 series. Thankfully, though, the rumors have already started coming, revealing key details about the phone.

Here's everything we know about the Samsung Galaxy S27 Pro so far.

200MP main, 50MP ultrawide, 10MP with 3x optical soom

The Galaxy S27 Pro is rumored to come with a 6.5-inch display, which will sit between the 6.3-inch Galaxy S27 and the 6.7-inch Galaxy S27 Plus. This effectively means that the S27 series will feature a whole range of screen sizes, letting you decide how big your phone wants to be.

While the S27 Ultra is expected to come with Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset, leaks claim the Pro will be missing out. Instead it should pack the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6, the direct successor to the Gen 5 chip that powers most flagship Android phones.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Beyond this we don't know that much about the chip in question, other than the fact it won't be as powerful as the Extreme variant. Presumably Samsung will opt for a custom "for Galaxy" chip that offers more performance power than the standard model, and it's guaranteed to be faster than the Gen 5 chip. But that's all we know for the time being.

It's safe to say that the S27 Pro will have 12GB of RAM, at least on the models with smaller storage variants. RAM costs are through the roof, and Samsung is one of many phone makers that is limiting 16GB of RAM to phones with at least 1TB of storage. That stinks for on-device AI, though it should help keep costs under control.

Like the rest of the S27 series, the Galaxy S27 Pro is expected to come with a triple-lens camera setup. According to database leaks the phone will have the same 200MP main camera lens are the Ultra, paired with a 50MP ultrawide lens and a 10MP telephoto lens capable of 3x optical zoom.

The selfie camera will reportedly user a 16MP sensor, with the Pro and Ultra featuring the same front-facing hardware.

There have been rumors that we could see a 12MP telephoto lens or one with 50MP resolution and 3.5x optical zoom. But considering the Pro model is supposed to be cheaper and less impressive than the Ultra, it makes sense that Samsung would nerf it by repurposing the secondary telephoto lens from the S26 Ultra for an extra year.

Like other Galaxy phones, we know that the Galaxy S27 Pro will have a heavy software focus, though we don't actually know what that might entail. We assume that the phone will run on OneUI 9.5, which is currently in early development, and Galaxy AI will likely play a large role in that update.

Beyond that, we have no idea what changes might be made, or what new software features Samsung will offer. So we'll just have to wait until Galaxy Unpacked to find out, or hope that the details leak between now and January.

Samsung is rumored to be utilizing silicon carbon batteries in the Galaxy S27 series, just as it did with the Z Fold 8 series. This means that the S27 Pro will likely have better battery density, allowing for more power to be squeezed into the same amount of space.

For that reason it's claimed that the S27 Pro will feature a 5,200 mAh battery, which is actually 200mAh more than we saw in the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Considering the screen is smaller, and the chip is likely more efficient, it'll be interesting to see how the battery life compares between the two phones.

Charging speed is expected to top out at 60W, with 25W wireless charging. On top of that, rumors claim that the S27 Pro and Ultra will be the only two phones to offer full Qi2 magnetic charging — without needing any special cases.

There's still a lot we don't know about the Samsung Galaxy S27 Pro, and only time can help fill in those gaps. It's likely that more rumors will appear in the coming weeks and months, helping to build a better picture of the phone, but until then we can only speculate as to what this device might have to offer.

That said, it is looking like the S27 Pro will be filling a small niche in the S27 lineup. Acting as a device for those people that want premium features, like high resolution cameras, but don't necessarily want to go overboard on the large (and expensive) Ultra model. It's a bold strategy from Samsung, especially since the S27 is expected to be more expensive than the S26 series, and only time will tell whether it will pay off.

It's all probably going to hinge on how its price compares to the Ultra and Plus models.

#3128. How Microcredentials Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI

IEEE Credentialing Program offers ethics and compliance training

Kaitlyn Ridel is the IEEE microcredentials marketing specialist.

Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate artificial intelligence, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level AI ethics, governance, and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges.

“AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance.

Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, and the International Organization for Standardization.

The regulations aim to mitigate issues such as systemic bias, security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks, but they also highlight a critical skills gap.

Most traditional computer science, software, and electrical engineering degree programs were built around technical design and system architecture. They do not yet include training in AI auditing, data tracking, or safety protocols for how AI systems interact with people and other technologies.

Expecting mid-career engineers to leave their job to attend a full-time two- or four-year program to learn about the topics is not feasible. Yet treating safety and governance as an afterthought can lead to costly product delays, legal exposure, and broken public trust.

Targeted microcredential programs can bridge the knowledge gap by helping engineers build skills in compliance, AI ethics, and governance.

Skills-based microcredentials represent the mastery of expertise gained through a learning program. To earn them, learners must demonstrate the skill through a validation assessment. The microcredentials can be stacked, showing a growing skill set in a defined area and allowing learners to earn several microcredentials in one program.

Microcredentials also allow engineers to upskill and master critical competencies, such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing, without interrupting their career. Through rigorous skills-validation assessments, microcredentials give tech leaders verifiable proof that their teams can audit systems effectively before deployment.

For engineering organizations, microcredentialing creates an agile upskilling pathway. It connects software engineering and hardware design directly to regulatory frameworks, empowering teams to certify systems for safety and compliance within their development life cycles.

Bridging technical capability and ethical responsibility requires a trusted foundation. IEEE has long been a pioneer in socio-technical standards, most notably through the IEEE 7000 series for ethics in AI system design, a framework created to address ethical considerations during the development life cycle.

The IEEE Credentialing Program translates the organization’s world-class standards into actionable, industry-aligned microcredentials. For more than three decades, IEEE has set the gold standard for technical validation and professional certification. By pairing cutting-edge AI governance standards with targeted microcredential programs, IEEE provides engineers and IT leaders with clear, standardized road maps to build systems that are not just technically advanced but also safe, compliant, and worthy of public trust.

To learn more about the credentialing program, explore the offerings or connect with an IEEE expert.

Kaitlyn Ridel is a marketing specialist for the IEEE Microcredentialing Program

Google just launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen, and it could be one of the biggest upgrades to its free AI chatbot yet.

The new model, announced Thursday, is designed to be faster, more accurate and better at following instructions. It even edges out Google's more expensive Gemini 4 Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, scoring 51 compared with Argon's 50 at Hydrogen's default high reasoning setting.

But the real reason to pay attention is what Hydrogen could mean for everyday Gemini users.

Google says the model is better at handling complicated requests, working with information across different apps and producing useful results without endless follow-up prompts. The company also claims it reduces fabricated information by more than fivefold compared with Gemini 3.8 Flash in its evaluations.

And unlike Google's most powerful Gemini models, Hydrogen is available to free users, although there's a catch. You won't necessarily be able to select it manually without a subscription. Instead, Google's automatic model selection determines when Hydrogen is appropriate for your request.

Here are five ways to put Google's newest AI to work.

Most AI models are good at summarization and pulling out the most important points from documents. But Google says this model in particular can process dense PDFs, spreadsheets, charts and other complicated material, pulling relevant details into organized reports and summaries. So, it doesn't only summarize, but it can then implement the information into something you can use. That means you could upload a lengthy insurance policy, school handbook or appliance manual and ask Gemini to find the information you actually need.You can also ask follow-up questions without having to explain the document all over again.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

Prompt to try: Read this document and explain the 10 most important things I need to know in plain English. Highlight any deadlines, fees, restrictions or potential problems. Include page references for every important finding and create a table of anything that requires action.

One of the biggest frustrations with AI writing is getting something that sounds natural rather than a generic corporate announcement.

Google says Hydrogen is significantly better at following detailed instructions about tone, length, formatting and style. In theory, that means less time rewriting the same email five different ways.

Try giving it a difficult writing task, such as responding diplomatically to an unreasonable request or explaining something complicated without sounding condescending.The key is giving Gemini specific rules about what you want and what you don't want.

Prompt to try: Help me write a friendly but firm email declining a request. Keep it under 150 words. Make it sound warm, confident and conversational, not overly formal. Avoid corporate jargon, unnecessary apologies and long introductions. Explain my decision clearly and end on a positive note.

This is one of my favorite uses for Hydrogen because it uses the applications you use most within Google Workspace.

Google says the model is better at connecting information from uploaded files, Gmail, Google Drive and supported connected apps, including services such as Dropbox and Airtable. Just keep in mind that you'll need to connect the relevant apps and grant Gemini permission to access them first. Access to individual integrations and actions can also depend on your account and subscription.

Rather than searching through messages individually, you could ask Gemini to piece together information from several sources and turn it into an actionable plan. I've already used it for organizing my busy family schedule and pulling together information for an upcoming project.

Prompt to try: Look through my connected Gmail and Google Drive for information about my upcoming appointments and events over the next two weeks. Create a chronological schedule with dates, times, locations and anything I need to prepare. Flag missing information and tell me which emails or documents contain the details.

Hydrogen isn't just designed to answer questions. Google has also improved its ability to turn plain-English instructions into working interactive projects.

The company demonstrated the model building everything from an interactive 3D globe that visualizes lightning strikes to a virtual island where people can create structures using simple prompts. You don't need to attempt anything nearly that ambitious, but you could ask Gemini to build a household budget calculator, an interactive study guide or a simple game.What I think is cool is what happens after the first version. You can ask Gemini to change colors, add features or fix problems using ordinary language. Keep reiterating to get the best results. In fact, I recommend giving this a try in Gemini's Canvas so you can keep your project organized.

Prompt to try: Create a simple, interactive household budget calculator with fields for monthly income, housing, groceries, utilities, transportation and savings. Automatically calculate the amount remaining after expenses. Include a visual chart and make the design clean, colorful and easy to use on a phone. Show me how to preview and use it.

Hydrogen isn't limited to the Gemini app. Google is also bringing the model to Search, where it says users should see better responses to complicated questions.

Instead of requiring a perfectly worded search, Hydrogen is designed to understand what you're actually trying to accomplish, even when your request includes multiple questions or confusing details.

Google also says its upgraded Search system can discover a wider range of relevant sources and present information in more useful visual formats. The goal is to make Search better at understanding the entire request rather than treating it as a collection of keywords.

Search to try: I need a lightweight laptop for working from coffee shops that has excellent battery life, can handle lots of browser tabs and costs less than $800. Compare my best options, explain the trade-offs and show me reliable reviews.

Head to the Gemini site and sign in with your Google account.

Google is rolling out Hydrogen globally, but the exact experience depends on your subscription. Free users can access Hydrogen through automatic model selection, which chooses the model based on the complexity of the request. Most straightforward questions may still use a lighter model.

If you don't see Hydrogen listed in your model picker, that doesn't necessarily mean you aren't using it. With automatic selection enabled, Google can route appropriate requests to Hydrogen.

Gemini 4 Hydrogen is not Google's most powerful AI model, but I've already experienced what it can do for everyday tasks. Its improvements focus on the things people actually do with AI: understanding documents, writing emails, organizing information, researching purchases and creating useful tools for their life.

Give it a try and let me know in the comments what you think.

#3124. iOS 27’s Find My app adds convenient feature I’ve long wished for

iOS 27 is packed with new features, including several for the Find My app. One upgrade to Find My—custom sharing durations—grants a feature request I’ve had for years.

Apple’s Find My app is a great way to share your location with friends or family members on either permanent or a temporary basis.

But the “temporary” option just got a very welcome upgrade in iOS 27.

That’s because you can now set up location sharing in Find My for a custom duration. Per Apple:

users [now] have more control over how they share their location with friends and family using Find My, with new options to share for a custom duration — either for a number of minutes, hours, or days — or even set a date and time for when sharing will stop. This makes it easy for users to share their location while attending an event, or for a long weekend getaway with friends and family.

Until iOS 27, you could only choose from a very limited set of “temporary” options for sharing: for one hour, or until end of day. The only other option was “indefinitely.”

The main time I find myself adding new people to share my location with, I’m either traveling or they’re visiting me. On these occasions, the “one hour” and “until end of day” options never cut it.

So of course, I have to choose “indefinitely.” Then there’s the decision after the trip ends of either continuing to let location sharing happen, or ending sharing immediately (if I remember to). And the latter option has always felt a little awkward to me. I’d much rather schedule the sharing duration upfront.

And now with iOS 27 I can. When sharing location with someone, a new ‘Custom’ duration option allows choosing an end date and time, and/or manually setting a given number of days, hours, and minutes for sharing to continue.

It’s a great change, long overdue, and works perfectly for the scenarios Apple outlined.

Have you ever wished for custom sharing durations in Find My? Let us know in the comments.
