#3123. Saatva Natural Latex Mattress Topper review: ‘After one week, I’m convinced it’s the perfect topper to soften up a firm mattress’

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Saatva Natural Latex Mattress Topper is small but mighty, providing a softening top layer to firm beds, despite its 1.5" depth. I slept on a king size topper on top of my medium-firm Plushbeds Botanical Bliss Organic Latex Mattress for a week, and felt immediate added pressure relief across my shoulders, hips and knees. It also helps provide cushioning around my lumbar, preventing a build-up of pain in that area. Plus, its natural materials wick away moisture for breathable sleep. For its $345 queen price, it comes with a 6-month trial run, which is more than most.

Made from natural latex and cotton for breathable sleep

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

As someone who has tested some of the best mattresses and the best mattress toppers you can buy, I can confidently say that the Saatva Natural Latex Mattress Topper is an excellent, naturally cooling choice for softening up firm beds. I slept on a king size Saatva Natural Latex Mattress Topper on top of my medium-firm Plushbeds Botanical Bliss Organic Latex Mattress for a week and felt an immediate increase in pressure relief across my shoulders, hips and knees.

Type: Natural latexDepth: 1.5 inchesCover: CottonCorner straps: YesTrial period: 180 nightsWarranty: 1-year warrantyStarting MSRP: from $255 (Twin) at Saatva

I've tested some of best Saatva mattresses, and all but one were on the firmer side. It’s no wonder that the brand offers the Saatva Natural Latex Topper because after one week, I’m convinced that it’s the perfect topper to soften up a firm mattress.

Not only is this topper incredibly comfortable and pressure relieving, but it’s supportive enough to sleep on my stomach and back, with enough give to sleep on my side too. Both the natural latex and cotton cover were breathable and kept my temperature neutral throughout the night, so I didn’t wake up hot or sweaty.

On one hand, the 1.5" height won’t require you to buy deeper sheets, however, it may not be thick enough for larger bodies. I should also mention that the topper didn’t quite cover my mattress from one edge to the other. The cover isn’t removeable, and thus washable, but at least it has an antimicrobial treatment to prevent mold and mildew growth.

Overall, I think it’s a solid topper for those who sleep hot or want to soften their firm mattress without making it too soft. Keep reading for my full breakdown of this topper to see if it’s a good choice for you.

The Saatva Natural Latex Mattress Topper starts out at $255 for a twin size, with a queen priced at $345. The premium price tag is not surprising, considering the topper is made with natural latex. However, we’ve seen more expensive natural latex toppers from Naturepedic ($399 for a queen at full MSRP) and Brooklyn Bedding ($587.07 for a queen on sale) so the Saatva is comparatively excellent value for money.

The price of the Natural Latex Topper includes free shipping, a one-year warranty, and a 180-night sleep trial with free returns.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

We track the best Saatva mattress sales all year round and have never seen this topper on sale, so you don't have to wait for the best time to buy — this is it.

The Saatva Natural Latex Mattress is 1.5" tall, which is a nice height because I can still use my regular sheets without any issue. Although natural latex is more breathable than memory foam, the perforations in this topper result in even better airflow. The cotton cover helps with breathability and has moisture wicking properties too.

Neither the latex nor the cotton cover is organic, but at least the latex foam is eco-INSTITUT® and Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) certified. Saatva also added a Guardin™ botanical antimicrobial treatment which prevents bacteria, mold, and mildew growth. This is a nice perk considering the cover is not removeable.

You can order the topper in any mattress size, but keep in mind that the topper didn’t quite cover my entire king-size mattress. There was about one to two inches of my mattress peeking out on either side of the topper. With the four straps holding the topper in place, I was able to guide it to the center of my mattress.

The only other drawback to the design was the extra fabric that was noticeable when I removed it from the packaging and at the end of testing. I couldn’t feel the fabric sticking up or bunching as I slept, but it’s quite noticeable when the sheets are off the mattress.

I slept on the Saatva Latex Mattress Topper for one week and tested everything from temperature regulation to comfort. Here’s what I found:

Setting the Saatva Latex Mattress Topper on my bed took five minutes to complete. It arrived vacuum-sealed and rolled up into a small box. The box was pretty damaged but thankfully that did not affect the topper.

Upon removing the plastic, the topper unraveled and expanded. I moved it onto the center of the mattress and noticed that there were a few inches on either side of the mattress, even when it was strapped into place with the corner straps. There was also a lot of extra fabric that bunched up from the cover. The topper had already expanded so I knew right away that the latex wasn’t going to fill out the cover and that for some reason there was just too much fabric.

Memory foam off-gasses and causes smells, but since this topper is made from latex, there were no smells. I slept on the mattress topper that night.

I sleep on an organic natural latex mattress, so when I placed the Saatva Latex Mattress Topper on my mattress to test, the topper was slightly softer than my mattress. After a week of testing, I’d say the topper offers a medium-soft feel that’s a 5.5 out of 10 on the firmness scale. The surface didn’t contour around my body, and I didn’t sink into the topper. Instead, it provided a hug-like feel, one that relieved pressure across the touch-points of the bed as I slept. My body felt supported and my spine was aligned no matter if I slept on my stomach, back, or side.

I’d suggest using this topper on a firm mattress that’s 7.5 or more out of 10 on the firmness scale, as the topper will provide a more cushioned and comfortable sleep experience, while maintaining the support you need. It could be used on a super soft mattress to extend its life. However, if you're paying $345 to provide extra comfort to a mattress that's lost its support, you could always consider picking up one of the best cheap mattresses instead for around the same price.

I tested the Saatva Latex Mattress Topper in Texas at the end of October and the beginning of November when the temperatures were in the high 70s or low 80s during the day and the low 70s and high 60s at night.

During this time, I turned my air conditioner off and used a fan to sleep at night, though it was still fairly warm in my house (about 70-76 degrees). I didn’t have to worry about overheating because the Saatva Natural Latex Mattress Topper was very breathable and maintained a temperature neutral sleep.

As someone who sleeps on a latex mattress, I expected to have this experience with the topper too, and I was glad to be right. No matter the time of year, I’m confident that the airflow through the perforated latex will ensure a sweat- and heat-free night of sleep.

At first glance, the Saatva Natural Latex Mattress Topper appears to have a 4.7-star rating out of 305 reviews on the Saatva site. However, a closer look shows that all the topper reviews are mixed together, so I wouldn’t trust that rating.

I was able to search the reviews for those who had specifically mentioned buying the Natural Latex Mattress Topper and found reviewers who liked the topper because of its pain-relieving qualities, especially when placed on firmer mattresses.

Because of how the reviews section is designed, it was not easy to find lower-star rating reviews of the Saatva Natural Latex Mattress Topper. Even so, I found a few customers who weren’t fans of the topper, with some stating that the 1.5" thickness flattened too quickly or that the topper developed creases.

✅ Your mattress is too firm: If you love the supportive aspects of a firm mattress but don’t want to wake up with aches and pains, the Saatva Latex Mattress Topper can help. The medium soft feel is comfortable and provides just enough cushioning, while also being supportive.

✅ You overheat at night: The cotton cover and the natural latex work well together to provide a temperature neutral sleep. You won’t get this kind of airflow with a memory foam topper.

✅ You and your partner have different sleep needs: The Saatva Latex Mattress Topper is ideal for any sleep type and those who sleep hot. If your partner likes a firm bed, but you don’t, this topper will provide some cushioning that you need, while maintaining the firm feel your partner likes.

❌ You are trying to firm up your mattress: If you’re trying to provide some more support to your soft mattress or firm it up a bit, the Natural Latex Mattress Topper has too much flexibility.

❌ You prefer a contouring topper or a sink-in feel: Natural latex is a somewhat bouncy material, so you aren’t going to sink into the Natural Latex Mattress Topper or feel the material contour around your body. This topper has more of a cloud-like feel that keeps your body lifted.

❌ You want a washable, removable cover: This mattress topper is spot-clean only – but at least it has a Guardian antimicrobial treatment that can prevent the growth of mildew, bacteria, and mold.

There’s a lot to love about the Brooklyn Bedding 3” Latex Topper, like how it comes with a removable and washable cotton cover and is cool to the touch. When buying the three-inch thick topper, you choose between a soft, medium, or firm feel. The three-year warranty is great, especially considering the high price.

The Naturepedic Adagio Organic Latex Mattress is half an inch taller than the Saatva topper and one of the most comfortable toppers that Tom’s Guide has ever tested. Unfortunately, it lacks straps, but at least its certified organic and is a great option for back, stomach and side sleepers. Learn more in our Naturepedic Adagio Organic Latex Mattress Topper review.

The Birch Plush Organic Mattress Topper is expensive but it’s a good choice for those who want a latex topper to firm up their soft mattress. You’ll enjoy similar benefits to the Saatva Natural Latex Topper, like breathability and support, but at least the Birch Plush Organic Topper has a 10-year warranty.

Alex Temblador is a freelance mattress reviewer and writer who has tested a range of traditional and smart mattresses for Tom's Guide. Alex also reviews bedding and other sleep products for Tom's Guide, including the Brooklinen All-Season Down Comforter and the BeautyRest Black Luxury Foam Pillow. Elsewhere, Alex's work has been published at Dwell, Real Homes, Architectural Digest, and Gardeningetc. When Alex isn’t reviewing sleep and home products, she’s building her career as the award-winning author of two novels, Secrets of the Casa Rosada and Half Outlaw, from her home base in Dallas, Texas.

#3121. Lazio-Reggina, Gentile sulla multiproprietà: «Vedrete, le cose andranno in porto»

Il legale di Lotito indica la strada per superare il divieto di multiproprietà e si dice ottimista sul futuro della Reggina.

Lazio e Reggina, la questione della multiproprietà torna al centro dell'attenzione. A parlarne è l'avvocato Gian Michele Gentile, legale di fiducia del presidente biancoceleste Claudio Lotito, che mostra grande ottimismo sulla possibilità di superare l'attuale ostacolo.

CLICCA QUI E SEGUI LAZIOPRESS.IT ANCHE SU INSTAGRAM

La strada indicata passa attraverso una riforma delle NOIF, che permetterebbe di modificare l'attuale situazione relativa alla multiproprietà. Gentile guarda già alla scadenza fissata al termine della stagione e utilizza parole particolarmente significative: «Vedrete che le cose programmate andranno in porto».

Secondo quanto riportato da Radio Touring 104, Gentile ha affrontato la questione nel corso di un'intervista nella quale ha parlato anche dell'operazione Reggina, delle motivazioni di Lotito e delle prospettive della società calabrese.

Il legale del presidente della Lazio ha spiegato quale sarebbe la strada per affrontare il problema della multiproprietà, collegandola anche alla possibilità di valorizzare maggiormente i calciatori italiani.

«Multiproprietà? L'ostacolo si supera con una riforma delle Noif. Secondo l'idea di Claudio Lotito, è un modo per valorizzare calciatori italiani in ottica Nazionale. Prendendo spunto dalla Salernitana. Con calciatori arrivati dalla Serie C fino alla Serie A. Poi Lotito ha dovuto svendere la Salernitana. L'obiettivo della riforma è di far partecipare e crescere numerosi calciatori, che non avrebbero tale possibilità se continuassero a giocare in traballanti realtà di Lega Pro. Senza sbocchi professionali. Non è una riforma per Lotito».

Gentile ha quindi affrontato direttamente l'investimento effettuato sulla Reggina, ribadendo le intenzioni del presidente biancoceleste.

«Lotito non fa le cose tanto per farle. Se ha preso la Reggina, è per farle ottenere il miglior risultato. Il problema sarà quello di eliminare il divieto di multiproprietà. Una riforma consentirebbe l'accesso alla Serie C».

Dietro l'operazione ci sarebbe stata anche una componente sentimentale, legata alle origini della famiglia Lotito.

«La trattativa per la Reggina è stata sentimentale. La famiglia di Lotito ha origini calabresi. Il sindaco di Reggio Calabria ha premuto moltissimo per raggiungere un accordo».

Il legale ha poi ricostruito alcuni aspetti della situazione economica trovata al momento dell'operazione.

«Abbiamo verificato la situazione, sia pure sommariamente. La società che fa capo a Lotito si è impegnata a sanare le passività. Tutto nel giro di 10 o 15 giorni, con grande soddisfazione di tutti».

Gentile ha specificato anche la natura delle pendenze: «Stipendi non pagati e anticipazioni degli ex soci. Roba ordinaria, compatibile con la gestione di una società di calcio in difficoltà sportiva».

Infine, un'altra precisazione: «La Rhegium è stata creata da Lotito».

Clearly, the experience didn’t sour Pitt on the relationship. Or if it did, F1 becoming a huge theatrical hit helped patch things up.

Apple TV is available for $14.99 per month, or you can get it discounted through the Apple One bundle.

#3118. Top Wall Street analysts prefer these dividend stocks for boosting portfolio returns

Dividend stocks remain a popular choice for investors seeking steady income and higher portfolio returns. However, with thousands of dividend-paying companies to choose from, identifying the right stocks can be challenging.

In this regard, recommendations from top Wall Street analysts can provide useful insights and help identify dividend stocks backed by solid fundamentals and with attractive upside potential.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Independent oil and natural gas company Permian Resources (PR) is this week's first dividend stock. The company recently paid a quarterly base cash dividend of 16 cents per share. At an annualized dividend of 64 cents per share, PR offers a dividend yield of 3.5%.

Recently, Evercore analyst Chris Baker initiated coverage of Permian Resources stock with a price target of $25. The analyst believes that the company is well positioned to benefit from improving U.S. shale demand after the Iran conflict, thanks to its low-breakeven inventory that can boost free cash flow growth. Baker also noted PR's disciplined consolidation in the Permian Basin.

Furthermore, the 5-star analyst highlighted the company's focus on a single basin and management's efficient capital allocations across expansion efforts, strategic acquisitions, and share buybacks. Baker noted that management focuses investments on the higher-return Northern Delaware Basin, helping boost profitability.

"The key piece of our work here, and the reason we think PR deserves a higher multiple relative to more finite or less flexible shale stories, is that PR runs an acquire and exploit model," said Baker.

He explained that Permian Resources deserves a premium valuation as it continually acquires and develops new high-quality assets instead of relying on a limited inventory, a strategy that is the market is underappreciating.

Baker ranks No. 862 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 75% of the time, delivering an average return of 48.3%. See Permian Resources Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Valero Energy (VLO) is a manufacturer and marketer of petroleum-based and low-carbon liquid transportation fuels and petrochemical products. At a quarterly dividend of $1.20 per share, or annualized dividend of $4.80 per share, VLO stock offers a yield of about 2%.

Heading into Valero's second-quarter earnings on July 30, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on VLO stock and increased the price target to $286 from $283 to reflect updated estimates.

Specifically, the 5-star analyst raised his 2026 and 2027 earnings per share estimates to $31.42 and $23.07 from $29.42 and $21.06, respectively, while leaving the 2028 EPS estimate unchanged at $20.37. Mehta made these revisions based on several factors, including updated commodity price assumptions and changes to refining capture rates.

Despite a strong year-to-date rally in VLO stock, Mehta still finds it compelling due to his more positive refining outlook. Moreover, the analyst sees the possibility of solid estimate revisions, which could drive the stock higher. He believes that Valero is well-positioned to benefit from improving refining market conditions due to its strong position in the Gulf Coast, solid balance sheet strength, and low-cost operations.

"Additionally, we believe the company's premium asset portfolio and crude slate optionality should support capture rates and stronger cash flow generation in the near-term, ultimately supporting shareholder returns," said Mehta.

Mehta ranks No. 742 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 59% of the time, delivering an average return of 10.2%. See Valero Energy Statistics on TipRanks.

Moving on to Ovintiv (OVV), a North American oil and natural gas producer. It has solid positions in North America's premier oil basins – the Permian and the Montney. OVV offers a quarterly dividend of 30 cents per share, or an annualized dividend of $1.20 per share, implying a 2.3% yield.

Following meetings with management, RBC Capital analyst Gregory Pardy reaffirmed a buy rating on Ovintiv stock with a price target of $70, highlighting that the stock is on RBC's Global Energy Best Ideas List.

"In our eyes, the depth of Ovintiv's Montney position, streamlined portfolio, strong balance sheet and enhanced shareholder returns afford investors with an attractive valuation re-rating opportunity over time," said Pardy.

The 5-star analyst stated that his meetings with management bolstered his confidence in the company's outlook and potential to achieve a higher valuation. Pardy noted Ovintiv's transformation, with the company streamlining its portfolio from six basins (including the Uinta, Bakken and Anadarko) to two – the Montney and Permian – while enhancing the depth of its inventory.

Pardy also emphasized OVV's improved shareholder returns and solid balance sheet following the recent sale of its assets in the Anadarko Basin for $3 billion.

Pardy ranks No. 169 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 22.3%. See Ovintiv Options Trading Activity on TipRanks.

#3117. Opera One for iOS adds Data Saver feature, cutting browsing data usage by up to 80%

Opera today announced that its Data Saver feature is now available on iOS, in a press release that also revealed a 20% year-over-year increase in the browser’s monthly active users. Here are the details.

In a press release published today, Opera celebrated a 20% year-over-year increase in monthly active users on iOS last month, “building on its established presence in Asia and Africa while expanding its reach in the US and Europe.”

In the US alone, growth was even stronger, with monthly active users increasing 46% year over year.

In both cases, that outpaced the 16% year-over-year growth Opera reported on PC just a few days ago, when the company also announced it had surpassed 100 million monthly active users for the first time.

Behind this growth across both desktop and mobile is a broader shift in consumer expectations – users are increasingly reconsidering the default as their understanding of what a browser can do evolves.

In today’s announcement, Opera also touted the arrival of Data Saver on Opera One for iOS, which the company says can reduce browsing data usage by up to 80% by compressing images and text on its servers before they reach the user’s device.

For users, this can make a difference when travelling abroad on expensive roaming data, topping up a prepaid plan or running low on a monthly data bundle. Data Saver can also help when browsing on a weak connection.

#3116. Apple HomeView launches tomorrow, but its first security update is already here

While the first HomeView units won’t reach customers until tomorrow, Apple today released a software update addressing nine security vulnerabilities. Here are the details.

Apple today released HomeView Software Version 27.2 (build 24V526), which contains some of the security fixes the company included in recent updates to its other operating systems, including iOS 27.2, macOS 27.2 Golden Gate, and iPadOS 27.2.

These include a vulnerability that could allow a remote attacker to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages, as well as another that could allow a malicious Bluetooth device to pair without user interaction.

In practice, this means that users who get the device starting tomorrow are advised to update it as soon as possible, since the vulnerabilities have been publicly disclosed.

Here’s the full security content of HomeView Software Version 27.2

Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts

Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management.

Impact: An app may be able to access sensitive user data

Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved state management.

Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to corrupt process memory

Description: A use-after-free issue was addressed with improved memory management.

Impact: Processing maliciously crafted input may lead to memory corruption

Description: An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved input validation.

Impact: A malicious Bluetooth device may be able to establish a pairing without user interaction

Description: This issue was addressed with improved checks.

Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts and pair with a device without user interaction

Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management.

Impact: A remote attacker may be able to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages

Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved validation.

Impact: A user added to an iMessage group may be able to access messages sent before they joined

Description: This issue was addressed by removing the vulnerable code.

Impact: An attacker on the same network may be able to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing code attempts

Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management.

Earlier today, Apple also confirmed that a software update coming next month will add support for security accessories to HomeView’s Siri AI, which currently refuses to unlock doors or open garage doors via voice commands.

Be sure to catch 9to5Mac’s full review of Apple HomeView ahead of tomorrow’s launch.

#3114. Apple TV just debuted three new originals, including a heist thriller series

Up first is “Being Heumann,” which tells the true story of how Judy Heumann led a 1977 protest that resulted in the longest occupation of a federal building in US history.

The movie is directed by Siân Heder, whose previous film, “CODA,” earned Apple its first Academy Award for Best Picture, in addition to winning Best Adapted Screenplay for Heder and Best Supporting Actor for Troy Kotsur.

The premiere of “Being Heumann” also marks the debut of Apple TV’s new sign language accessibility feature, which allows viewers to watch select titles with an American Sign Language (ASL) or British Sign Language (BSL) interpreter appearing in the corner of the screen.

In addition to “Being Heumann,” the feature is also available for “F1 The Movie,” with “Greyhound” and “Way of the Warrior Kid” gaining support later this year. The latter premieres November 25.

The first two episodes of Apple’s anticipated heist thriller series “12 12 12” are now available.

Starring Anthony Mackie (Captain America: Brave New World) and Jamie Dornan (Belfast), the series also features Patrick Fabian (Better Call Saul) and Kali Reis (True Detective: Night Country), among others.

Here’s Apple TV on the new show, which will release new episodes every Friday through December 25:

Each episode of “12 12 12” unfolds across three timelines of a heist: the 12 months of planning, the 12 hours of the heist and the 12 days following it. The series follows a disgraced FBI agent (Anthony Mackie) and an American career criminal (Jamie Dornan) as they play a zero-sum game of cat and mouse across Europe. At the center of it all is the daring, epic raid on a bank vault deep beneath the streets of Zurich.

The first of two holiday specials coming to Apple TV this season, “Snoopy Presents: 12 Days of Snoopy” is now also available to stream, the other one being “Fraggle Rock: A Holiday Gift,” which arrives December 4.

The premiere marks the latest release under Apple’s ongoing partnership with Peanuts, and joins a growing collection of original Peanuts productions, alongside classics such as “A Charlie Brown Christmas,” “A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving,” and “It’s the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown.”

In fact, “A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving” is free to stream on the platform this weekend, meaning even those without an Apple TV subscription can watch it.

Back to “Snoopy Presents: 12 Days of Snoopy,” it follows Snoopy as he tries to get off Santa’s naughty list in the 12 days leading up to Christmas, learning along the way that “there’s more to Christmas than just getting gifts.”

#3113. New Apple TV 4K and HomeView now available: Here’s everything you need to know

The new Apple TV 4K and HomeView smart display are officially available. The first pre-orders have arrived for eager shoppers, and you can now also head to your local Apple Store to buy select configurations.

The new HomeView smart display gives you a way to interact with Siri AI, your HomeKit accessories, and more in a 7-inch square display form factor. It’s available in two versions. There’s one with a built-in base, and another that’s designed to be mounted on your wall.

HomeView is powered by an A18 chip and has a built-in 12MP Center Stage camera for FaceTime calls. It’s available in silver, starlight, rose pink, and space gray. You can read my full review for all the HomeView details you need.

When buying from Apple for delivery, HomeView in all four colors is backordered to the first week of December. Most Apple Stores, however, seem to have same-day pickup availability today, especially in silver and starlight. It costs $299.

On Amazon, HomeView is available for immediate delivery in Space Gray, Starlight, and Rose Pink. The silver model is backordered until later this month (and on the verge of selling out completely).

Meanwhile, the new Apple TV 4K is also available starting today. It’s powered by the A19 chip, up from the previous model’s A15 Bionic. It also has built-in far-field microphones, so you can now interact with Siri without using the remote.

The new Apple TV also supports Siri AI, enabling things like world knowledge and personal context requests. It’s worth noting that Siri AI is also coming to the second- and third-generation Apple TV 4K models via a software update.

The other flagship feature of the new Apple TV 4K is support for a four-HomePod surround sound system. You need four HomePod (2nd generation) or HomePod mini 2 speakers, arranged in matching pairs at the front and rear of the room.

Read my full review of the new Apple TV 4K for everything you need to know. The big takeaway, though, is that it costs $299, which may be hard for many shoppers to justify.

Will it be possible to use HomeView in countries beyond the launch locations? I understand it will operate only in English, but could I configure it with an iPhone set to another language? I do not require the Siri AI feature since it is unavailable in the EU; as a home hub it would still be valuable – if it works 😅

When buying from Apple’s Online Store for delivery, the new Apple TV 4K is backordered to the first week of December. Most Apple Stores appear to have some availability for walk-in purchases starting today.

On Amazon, the new Apple TV 4K is available for delivery as early as this weekend. You can also buy the new Siri Remote, which has a built-in speaker and Find My Precision Finding support, separately.

#3112. tvOS 27.2.1 launching soon with Siri AI for older Apple TV 4K models

Today the new Apple TV 4K has arrived (order here) with Siri AI as a major tentpole feature. But older Apple TV 4K models are about to get Siri AI too via a tvOS 27.2.1 software update.

Earlier this week, iOS 27.2.1 launched alongside companion updates like macOS 27.2.1, watchOS 27.2.1, and more.

Notably missing was tvOS 27.2.1. But the update’s absence now makes more sense, as Apple has confirmed that tvOS 27.2.1 introduces Siri AI support for select Apple TV 4K models.

Apple’s website has a newly updated support document that lists requirements for Siri AI on Apple TV. It says you need:

tvOS 27.2.1 on Apple TV 4K (2nd generation and later) and a Siri AI-enabled, paired device nearby

Although Apple has not yet specified launch timing for tvOS 27.2.1, it could launch as soon as today, or else early next week.

Because the new Apple TV 4K just now debuted, it’s understandable that Apple wouldn’t want to ship Siri AI for older models before the new one arrived.

As Apple’s website says, you’ll need a 2nd generation Apple TV 4K or later plus another paired Siri AI-enabled device, like a recent iPhone, to get the new Siri experience in tvOS.

To learn more about what Siri AI can do on Apple TV, read our review of the new Apple TV 4K here.

These five Netflix movies deserve a spot on your Christmas watchlist

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Christmas starts at the beginning of November for me, and I’m not ashamed to admit that my tree is already up. That means we’re officially entering my favorite time of year, when there’s nothing better than getting cozy, switching on the TV and settling in with a festive movie. If you’re anything like me, it’s never too early to start working through your Christmas watchlist, and Netflix has plenty of options to get you in the holiday spirit.

Whether you’re after a feel-good family adventure, a heartwarming romantic story or something with a little more star power, there’s a festive flick worth adding to your queue. I've rounded up five of the best Christmas movies streaming on Netflix right now, including favorites starring Kurt Russell, J.K. Simmons and Minka Kelly.

So grab a blanket, make yourself a hot chocolate and get comfortable. The countdown to Christmas is officially on.

“The Christmas Chronicles” is one of those festive films I find myself coming back to every year, and it's firmly part of my Christmas viewing tradition. Kurt Russell makes for a brilliantly unconventional Santa Claus, swapping the usual jolly grandfather image for something a little more street-smart, sarcastic and action-ready. Apparently, Russell even went as far as writing a 200-page backstory for the character, covering Santa’s history and his relationship with Mrs. Claus. It’s a fun twist on the familiar Christmas formula, and its popularity was strong enough to launch a sequel in 2020.

Siblings Kate (Darby Camp) and Teddy Pierce (Judah Lewis) come up with a plan to catch Santa Claus (Kurt Russell) on camera on Christmas Eve. After spotting him arriving at their home, the pair sneak aboard his sleigh, but their unexpected appearance causes it to crash in Chicago. With Santa’s reindeer scattered, his magical hat missing and his sack of presents lost, the children agree to help him recover everything before morning. Their night takes them on a chaotic adventure involving police chases, unexpected encounters and a visit to the North Pole, as they race against the clock to make sure presents reach children around the world.

“Klaus” is easily one of the most beautiful animated Christmas films out there, with its hand-drawn visuals giving it the feel of a storybook brought to life. It’s also a pretty remarkable success story, considering traditional studios initially passed on the project because 2D animation was seen as commercially outdated. Thankfully, Netflix gave it a home, and it went on to win seven Annie Awards, a BAFTA and an Oscar nomination for Best Animated Feature. I’d say it deserved every bit of that recognition. It’s a wonderfully heartfelt festive watch and one I always recommend adding to your Christmas movie lineup.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Spoiled postman-in-training Jesper (Jason Schwartzman) is sent to the remote, snow-covered town of Smeerensburg, where he must deliver 6,000 letters within a year or lose his family fortune. However, the miserable locals are locked in a bitter feud and have little interest in sending mail. Just as Jesper considers giving up, he meets Klaus (J.K. Simmons), a mysterious carpenter living alone in the woods with a cabin full of handmade toys. The pair strike a deal to deliver toys to the town’s children, but their growing popularity soon threatens to disrupt the locals’ long-standing rivalry.

I have to admit, 2025 turned out to be a surprisingly strong year for Netflix’s original Christmas movies, and “My Secret Santa” was one of the ones I genuinely enjoyed. Alexandra Breckenridge is a big part of its appeal, particularly if you know her from “Virgin River,” and it’s easy to see why Netflix wanted her front and centre in its festive lineup. There’s plenty of silly physical comedy and amusing disguise antics to keep things light, alongside the cozy romance you’d expect from a seasonal Netflix movie. It’s not reinventing the Christmas rom-com, but I had a good time with it.

When single mom Taylor Jacobson (Alexandra Breckenridge) loses her job just before Christmas, she finds herself struggling to make ends meet while trying to afford snowboarding lessons for her daughter. Desperate for work, Taylor hatches an unusual plan with the help of her friends: disguise herself as an elderly man and land a seasonal job playing Santa Claus at the luxury Sun Peaks ski resort. Her transformation works, and she soon finds herself entertaining holiday guests while working alongside resort manager Matthew Layne (Ryan Eggold). However, keeping her real identity under wraps becomes increasingly difficult.

“The Best Christmas Pageant Ever” is a lovely festive surprise, particularly if you’re after something a little different from the usual sugary holiday movies. Based on Barbara Robinson’s beloved 1972 children’s novel, this 2024 adaptation brings plenty of cheeky humor to its small-town Christmas setting while still delivering plenty of seasonal warmth. It also proved to be a sleeper hit at the box office, and its impressive Rotten Tomatoes scores speak for themselves, with 92% from critics and 97% from audiences. That’s a pretty strong endorsement for a Christmas movie, and I’d say it's well worth giving a chance.

Six troublesome siblings known as the Herdmans have a reputation for causing chaos wherever they go. But when they turn up at church looking for free snacks, they unexpectedly land the leading roles in the town’s annual Christmas pageant. First-time director Grace Bradley (Judy Greer) is left scrambling to keep the production on track, while her daughter Beth (Molly Belle Wright) watches as the newcomers turn rehearsals upside down. With the townspeople convinced the performance is destined for disaster, the Herdmans’ unconventional approach to the Nativity story leads to an unexpectedly memorable Christmas production.

“Champagne Problems” was another festive highlight from Netflix last year, quickly finding an audience with more than 20 million views in its opening week and topping the streamer’s global film chart. Director Mark Steven Johnson has clearly found his niche with these feel-good romantic comedies, having previously worked with Netflix on “Love, Guaranteed” and “Love in the Villa.” This one has all the ingredients of a Hallmark-style holiday romance, complete with a charming European setting and plenty of seasonal escapism. I’m always happy to start watching these sorts of films in mid-November, and this is exactly the kind of cozy pick I’m talking about.

Ambitious American executive Sydney Price (Minka Kelly) travels to Paris just before Christmas with an important career opportunity on the table: securing the acquisition of Château Cassell, a renowned French champagne house. After arriving, she takes a night off from negotiations to explore the city and meets a charming stranger named Henri (Tom Wozniczka). The pair hit it off, but their budding romance takes an unexpected turn when Sydney discovers Henri is the son of the champagne company’s founder. With several other potential buyers competing for the deal, Sydney heads to the family vineyard, where she must navigate the increasingly complicated negotiations.

Alix is a Senior Streaming Writer at Tom’s Guide, which basically means watching the best movies and TV shows and then writing about them. It’s a dream job for someone who’s been obsessed with storytelling since she first figured out how to work a remote.

Before joining Tom’s Guide, Alix honed her skills as a staff writer with outlets like Screen Rant and Bough Digital, where she discovered her love for the entertainment industry.

She heads to the cinema every week as a tradition, no matter what’s showing. For her, movies aren’t just entertainment — they’re a ritual, a comfort, and a constant source of inspiration. When she’s not at her desk or at the cinema, you’ll probably find her deep into a horror video game on her PC.

Shiny side, or dull side, that is the question

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Aluminum foil is a kitchen staple, and I'm not sure what I'd do without it. Okay, that is a tad dramatic, but it does come in super handy when I'm wrapping up my leftovers or protecting my pans.

There are even 7 surprising uses for aluminum foil that you might have never heard of that I use from time to time.

Despite having it in my kitchen for years, I've never really questioned why one side is distinctly shiny, while the other is dull. In fact, I've always just assumed that shiny side always goes down – and I'm not even sure why. But that doesn't make me right... or does it?

Whether you're a shiny-side-up or shiny-side-down kind of person, I'm going to settle the debate of which is actually right once and for all.

Before we get into resolving the debate though, I think it's important to explain exactly why aluminum has two different sides – and it's actually weirdly simple. To turn aluminum foil into the thin sheets we end up buying from the shops, large rollers pass two layers through at the same time to create that ultra-thin form.

This doubling effect means that the side that meets with the roller ends up with a shiny finish and the other side that presses against another layer ends up being dull. And that's it.

You want your aluminum foil to provide a barrier, help your food retain moisture when cooking, ensure the heat is distributed evenly by reflecting and conducting it and to just help with the overall clean-up when the food is ready to serve. But, does having a dull and shiny side actually make any difference when it's used in the kitchen?

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Can you ever really have enough aluminum foil? For jut over $15, you can grab 200 sq ft that's both freezer safe and grill safe, perfect for easy prep, cooking and clean-up. Cover up your leftovers or wrap up your sandwiches, foil is incredibly versatile and malleable, making it a staple of kitchens everywhere.

Whether you're creating a tent for large roasting meats, a packet to trap moisture and flavors, covering pots and pans or simply wrapping up a sandwich, I'm here to tell you it actually makes no difference if you use the shiny side or the dull side. It's just cosmetic.

In fact, some brands even state on the packaging that the aluminum foil will perform exactly the same, no matter which way you use it. And while there's a debate about the shiny side being more capable of heat reflection, it's a difference so small that it's not worth talking about.

While I have this innate urge to keep the dull side hidden, it's purely an aesthetic choice – and that's where it pretty much ends. There is one exception to the rule though and that's if you've purchased an aluminum foil that specifically states that it's 'non-stick'.

For this, a coating is often applied to the dull side of the foil meaning you want to the treated side to be touching your food to reduce the chance of burning or tearing (check your specific product for details on which side that is though).

But ultimately, having both a shiny side and a dull side is merely a product of the manufacturing process. Whether you use one or the other is entirely up to you. But, if you want to keep debating it with friends and family, watch out that they haven't already read this.

#3107. Security Bite: Apple details Secure Exclaves, a glimpse at its ambient computing future

9to5Mac Security Bite is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Making Apple devices work-ready and enterprise-safe is all we do. Our unique integrated approach to management and security combines state-of-the-art Apple-specific security solutions for fully automated Hardening & Compliance, Next Generation EDR, AI-powered Zero Trust, and exclusive Privilege Management with the most powerful and modern Apple MDM on the market. The result is a totally automated Apple Unified Platform currently trusted by over 45,000 organizations to make millions of Apple devices work-ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

Apple published a new security research post this week detailing Secure Exclaves, a new architecture built to handle what the company calls “ambient sensing.” The latter isn’t anything new. “Hey, Siri” has been using a version of this always-on listening technology for years. The difference now (particularly on newer devices like Apple Watch Series 12 and HomeView) is new features need far more data from your surroundings, and Apple has changed where that data gets processed.

Today, on most Apple hardware, wake-word detections run locally on-device on a smaller, low-power chip. But once it thinks it heard you say “Hey, Siri,” the main operating system gets involved to confirm and wake up the smart assistant for use. There’s nothing necessarily wrong with this process. The split second of audio is all processed locally and not sent to Apple servers.

The problem lies in Apple’s newer features that ask for a lot more from users than a wake word.

Person recognition on HomeView identifies who’s in the room by face and voice, and Siri Recap and Live Rewind need to keep a running sense of what’s been happening around you. That adds up to a constant stream of sensitive camera and mic data, and it needs a more secure way of being processed than anything Apple had before.

Much like the existing Secure Enclaves architecture for authentication, instead of passing operations to the main OS, Secure Exclaves (notice the x) run their own tiny, separate operating system. Raw data goes in and a simple “that’s Arin” or “that’s the wake word” is outputted back to the OS, everything else is thrown away. According to Apple, that data “cannot be accessed by the main operating system, apps, or Apple.”

The changes don’t stop there. In recent SB column, I mentioned how on iPhone, the green dot that appears indicating that the camera or mic is live is all software connected, not like the hardwired LED that exists on the Mac. Now on iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone Duo, and MacBook Neo, the camera and mic indicators now live inside this new exclave, meaning even a compromised OS shouldn’t be able to hide them for malicious purposes.

It’s apparent Apple is building toward this new level of ambient computing across every type of device when you read technical reports like this. Future AI-first products, like the heavily rumored AirPods Pro with inferred cameras, will most certainly built on this new Secure Exclave architecture.

This is the best laptop for video editing

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I preordered my 14-inch M1 Max MacBook Pro in October 2021, the week Apple announced it. It was my first Mac, and I documented the whole awkward leap in a video called "PC FanBoy Switches to NEW MacBook Pro - Should You?". Learning macOS as a complete noob was painful for several weeks, and it didn't really click until a few months later. But when it finally did, I got why creators love these things.

Five years later, it's the longest I've ever gone without "needing" a new laptop. It was one of my most expensive purchases at the time, but looking back all these years, probably one of the best investments I've ever made, despite how sad it made my bank statement look.

Since joining the Tom's Guide video team, my DaVinci Resolve projects have become far more demanding, with easily 8+ layers and several heavy GPU effects running at once. That finally caught up with my 5-year-old M1 Max, which now wheezes like it just climbed 10 flights of stairs. Every new MacBook Pro since has looked appealing, and I won't lie, I've had a few Apple shopping carts configured, but I never found it in me to hit that checkout button.

Then Apple announced the MacBook Pro with the PROLED XDR Display, and three things caught my eye: a tandem OLED screen (two OLED layers stacked for more brightness), a lighter body, and a touchscreen. Touch was the big keynote moment, but everything else made me ready to upgrade.

For the past two weeks, I've edited exclusively on the 16-inch MacBook Pro OLED in the M5 Max, 128GB, nano-texture configuration. Here's what the jump from my old 14-inch M1 Max with 32GB looks like.

The chip goes from M1 Max to M5 Max, and the memory quadruples. The screen grows from 14 inches to 16. I've wished for that bigger screen for years, but I always talked myself out of a 16-inch because of the weight. This one weighs 4.1 pounds, about 0.6 pounds less than the previous 16-inch MacBook Pro.

My M1 Max is around 3.5 pounds, so for roughly 0.6 pounds more I get a much bigger display. It's the first time a 16-inch laptop felt worth it to me. The new screen is a big part of why: it's what makes the body lighter, thinner, and slightly smaller, even though the display is slightly larger than on the non-touch MacBook Pros. At 0.63 inches thick, it's a hair slimmer than the 0.66-inch non-touch model; the footprint is slightly smaller, and the display grows from 16.2 to 16.3 inches.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

Then there are ports. My M1 Max has Thunderbolt 4, and that's why my massive Dell 52-inch 6K monitor was always stuck at 60Hz. The new laptop has three Thunderbolt 5 ports (the faster version of the same USB-C connector), and my monitor finally runs at 144Hz. Wi-Fi also jumps to Wi-Fi 7 from the Wi-Fi 6 on my old Mac, giving me faster connectivity when I'm working on the go.

And don't forget the return of the glowing Apple logo on the lid. The last MacBook Pro with one was back in 2015, so I only ever admired it from the outside, like the cool kids' lunch table. Sure, I never actually saw it glow, but I'm finally sitting at the table.

But here's what's really important. This is the best laptop display I've ever tested. I ran the same video project on this and a non-OLED MacBook Pro, and the shadows and bright scenes make fine details and color editing more precise. Apple rates the panel at up to 2,000 nits, and our lab measured 1,949, the brightest laptop screen Tom's Guide has tested.

The nano-texture glass is one of the most important choices you'll make here. It's an anti-glare finish that costs $150 extra, and while Apple has offered it before, it's especially worth it on a touchscreen. The surface feels smoother and more premium under your finger, while the standard glass feels more resistant by comparison. It also hides fingerprints better.

It's also why I can finally work away from my desk. I never used to edit on the go or outside because the glare was so bad. This is my first laptop with nano-texture, and I finally get the hype. It's already come in clutch several times, letting me clearly see my screen in sunny rooms, under harsh office lights, and in the back of long Ubers on the way to my next meeting. I haven't noticed any difference in vibrancy compared to the non-nano version. The only real downside is the special cleaning cloth I now have to remember to carry.

The Dynamic Island is the other screen upgrade that's easy to miss. It replaces the notch, and it's smaller and way less annoying. On my M1 Max, menu bar icons would get hidden behind the notch. They still do at times on this one, but not as much since the cutout is smaller. The whole laptop looks more cohesive too. The pill matches the design language of other Apple products like the iPhone; the display's rounded corners now match the rounded corner at the top, and the bezel is thinner.

By comparison, the older non-touch MacBook Pro panels look dated. It's not perfect, though. There's still no Face ID, which is a bummer, and even with the smaller cutout, apps still can't go full-screen to the very top of the display. I'm betting it's at least another 3 years before Apple sorts out these remaining quirks.

32GB of RAM was plenty for the past few years. Then my timelines started stacking effects in layers, and I also recently began editing 8K footage from my Lumix S1R II mirrorless camera.

In my more complex Resolve edits, I'd hit the "out of memory" warning and have to close ALL my background tasks; at times, even that wasn't enough, and I'd have to close my project, reload it, and remove some effects or render them out separately. This is the bottleneck you never want.

Upgrading to 128GB is something I never thought I'd be saying anytime soon, but my workflow has quickly scaled up to it. On the new machine, I've only hit a memory limit when running several local AI models at once while working on a new website I'm creating.

Under my normal workload, my Resolve projects now comfortably use 80GB or more of RAM when they need it, and I can still keep Safari with 20-plus tabs, Lightroom, Photoshop, and other background apps open without a sweat. This kind of headroom is incredible and really opens the door to working on several creative projects at once, without the constant back-and-forth dance I used to do.

The new ProLED uses the same M5 Max chip found in the MacBook Pros that came out in March, but it's still been a huge speed upgrade for me. When testing a few of my projects and renders, everything seems about twice as fast, and some exports now finish in real time or faster, something I never experienced before.

And not to get too meta, but I even edited my ProLED review video on this new laptop and compared it directly to my M1 Max. Timeline scrolling was snappier, and my zooms, blurs, and subject tracking were almost instant. Text layers sitting behind depth maps, which would stall on my M1 Max, played back in real time at full timeline resolution without a stutter. To say I was excited to edit again is an understatement.

But let's circle back to the touchscreen, because honestly, I went in thinking I'd quickly forget about it. It's not an iPad replacement, and it's not trying to be one. There's no Apple Pencil support, which makes sense on a screen that doesn't fold flat. And while Apple did show off a number of demos where you can draw or play piano on this, I don't think that's really what this is for.

It took a bit of retraining my brain to remember "oh, this is a touchscreen," but within a few hours it started to feel natural, at least some of the time. There's no lag when I click or drag, and tapping the app I want or resizing a window was often quicker than chasing it with the cursor. Apple didn't completely overhaul macOS for touch, but small changes like the enlarged window controls help avoid misclicks.

Unsurprisingly, for precise work like rearranging or trimming a video timeline, I still use the trackpad and keyboard. For more interactive jobs, like adjusting a curve in Lightroom or quickly culling through my photo selects, it's handy. I realized the touchscreen made sense when I was going back and forth between this and my old laptop and caught myself reaching for the screen on my old Mac more than once.

Here's the thing: I don't need touch, and I can easily live without it. I'm sure most people would agree, so it's everything you're getting on top of touch that makes this new ProLED model so appealing.

But you're paying an extra $400 to get it, and that's before the $150 for nano-texture if you want the full package. $550 on its own is a laptop (a budget one, sure, but a full laptop). As I've shared, these upgrades finally sold me on retiring my old laptop, and the display and weight savings alone are worth the premium over the non-ProLED model.

That said, I would have loved to see a non-touch model for around $100 less, since I could do without it. I'm also curious if and when these display upgrades will come to other models, including the Air and maybe even the Neo. Who knows?

I'm sure there are plenty of prospective buyers attracted by the fancy new display and slimmer design who don't necessarily need the extra horsepower offered here, and they might get pushed to buy more "laptop" than they really need, especially since it's currently limited to the M5 Pro and M5 Max models.

That said, if you're a content creator like myself and want the best laptop display on Apple's best laptop to date, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display was worth the wait.

#3104. OpenAI launches ChatGPT Wallet, enabling ‘dot’ agents to make purchases

OpenAI is launching ChatGPT Wallet, which it says is “setting a new bar for secure payments by agents.”

ChatGPT Wallet works with OpenAI’s “dots” agent feature and includes a partnership with American Express, MasterCard, and Visa. Here’s how it works.

OpenAI says ChatGPT Wallet is the “first wallet that lets agents pay without access to users’ actual card details and that requires a security check for every purchase, while also preserving existing card rewards and protections for eligible disputes.”

“We’re starting with limited availability to ChatGPT Pro users,” OpenAI explains, “so we can learn from real-world use and work with businesses, banks, and payment networks to improve compatibility and reliability.”

The feature won’t work with websites that block agents, however, which has increasingly become an issue online.

Before each purchase, the user reviews the items, total, and selected card, then approves it with a security check such as Face ID or a fingerprint scan. Each approval creates a clear record of the purchase the user authorized the agent to make.

After the user approves, the payment network provides a payment token—a substitute for the user’s actual card details—with a card number, security code, and expiration date. The payment is charged to their selected card without ChatGPT Wallet sharing their actual card details with the business or agent.

You can read more about ChatGPT Wallet and how it works here.

The company emphasizes that payments are secure, card info isn’t shared with your dot or merchants, and that you’re in control of purchases.

However, it still trades at a relative discount of 19% compared to EPD, which is below its historical discount range of 17%-20%. Furthermore, Smith expects the current energy market to support a stronger outlook for natural gas liquids and crude oil. "The current energy macro backdrop positions ET to benefit in all three commodities," said the analyst.

He expects Energy Transfer's adjusted EBITDA to grow at a 4.8% compound annual growth rate in 2027-2030, which is 1%-3% above Wall Street's expectations. In fact, Smith sees the possibility of additional upside if ET announces more natural gas projects. He added that investors will await details on final investment decisions on new natural gas projects and any clues about additional projects in the pipeline. The analyst noted that ET has announced new gas projects consistently in recent quarters.

Ahead of Q2 earnings, Jefferies analyst Lloyd Byrne reiterated a buy rating on Chevron stock and lowered his price target to $216 from $236. Byrne expects the company to report adjusted EPS of about $5.86 per share, nearly 9% above the Street's expectations.

The 5-star analyst highlighted that the challenges seen in Chevron's upstream business in the first quarter due to the disruption at the Tengizchevroil joint venture in Kazakhstan, Storm Fern downtime, and the Middle East conflict have largely been resolved. Consequently, Byrne expects production to recover in the second quarter to about 4,033 mboepd. He expects the upstream business to generate adjusted earnings of about $8.1 billion in Q2 2026.

Meanwhile, Byrne expects Chevron to generate downstream adjusted earnings of about $4.4 billion in Q2, with strength in both domestic and international markets. The downstream business benefited from higher crack spreads and strong refining performance.

Additionally, the analyst expects Chevron to generate $18.2 billion in cash flow from operations (before working capital changes), driven by stronger earnings and about $2.2 billion in dividends from affiliated companies. Unlike the first quarter, Chevron is not expected to make a TCO loan repayment in Q2, providing an additional boost to cash flow.

iOS 27.2 arrived last month with new features for Messages, Apple TV, and more, plus two improvements for CarPlay. Here’s what’s new for CarPlay users.

Apple Podcasts in iOS 27.2 adds two new sections to the Home tab: ‘New Episodes’ and ‘Continue Playing.’

Essentially, Apple has rethought how the core ‘Up Next’ queue of its Podcasts app works.

Like you would expect, ‘New Episodes’ contains only the latest episodes from your favorite shows. But after you’ve started an episode, you’ll find it in the ‘Continue Playing’ row just below.

This overhaul to podcast management makes it easier to find the latest episodes of your shows and also pick up where you previously left off. I’m a big fan of the change.

Siri AI introduces a variety of upgrades in iOS 27.2, including two that carry over to CarPlay as well.

It can take some adjustment to remember that Siri AI is available in the car just like on iPhone. But CarPlay is an especially useful platform for Apple’s more powerful assistant.

It’s arguable whether this qualifies as an “improvement,” but it is a change worth mentioning. iOS 27.2 includes a new app icon for Apple Music, plus some minor design tweaks in the app.

These changes are related to the broader rebrand of Apple Music that was recently unveiled.

For more new features in CarPlay that debuted in iOS 27, see our coverage here.

If you haven't heard of "micromovement" routines, it's like exercise snacking, where you break up sedentary time with mini workouts or chunks of movement, like walks, bodyweight routines, or even a quick jog.

According to research from Yoga-Go, you may add eight years to your biological age if you spend a lot of time sitting, which can be eight hours a day or more, regardless of whether you still exercise daily.

Determined to start my day on the right foot, I decided to add a seven-minute bodyweight workout to my mornings, and this is what I did and didn't notice after 30 days.

A post shared by Tom's Guide Fitness (@tomsguidefitness)

The decision to stand rather than sit or to take the stairs over the escalator determines how much movement you fit into your day and how much energy you burn outside of workouts, also known as Non-Exercise Activity Thermogenesis, or NEAT.

Just because you fit a 45-minute HIIT workout into your day doesn't undo the impact of accumulated sitting time, so how often you get up and move about really does matter for your long-term health.

The movements below can help maintain functional strength, relieve stress, combat sedentary time, and move your muscles and joints, which increases oxygen-rich blood flow around the body.

Here's the routine I followed every morning for 30 days.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

I love functional compound bodyweight exercises because they target the main muscle groups in your body and they can still feel challenging. If you're short on time and just want to get some movement in while you can, 60 seconds of each move performed back-to-back gives you a seven-minute full-body workout before you've even brushed your teeth in the morning.

I love that I could work my chest, shoulders, arms, back, glutes, core and legs without picking up a single weight or worrying over getting to the gym. I hadn't fatigued myself enough that I couldn't then go to Pilates, the yoga studio, or out for a run later in the day, and I had woken up my muscles, oiled my joints and got fresh blood flow pumping around my body while lifting my heart rate. All before I had even showered.

I love functional compound bodyweight exercises because they target the main muscle groups in your body and they can still feel challenging.

However, it's progressive overload that moves the needle when building strength and muscle, which means increasing the challenge on your muscles as they adapt to a routine or exercise. For that reason, I didn't see any physical changes, as my body is very attuned to lifting weights and attending classes like Pilates.

After 30 days of repeating these exercises, I genuinely felt my form improving and I could squeeze out extra push-ups without dropping my knees during the final 20 seconds of each minute. I also noticed my mobility improved a little during the day because the squats helped wake up my hips, knees and ankles.

I have a bad left shoulder, which has been a problem area for a number of years. Performing shoulder squeezes everyday helped me reset my posture first thing and helped wake up the lazy stabilizer muscles on my left side. Coupled with regular Supermans, I felt more aware of my posture daily.

I really enjoyed how this routine was quick and accessible and helped me feel more energized going into my day. It only takes seven minutes to wake up your whole body and build some foundational, functional strength, so it's hard to see why I shouldn't keep it up.

Let me know if you'd give this routine a try by voting in the poll above.

#3098. Apple Maps in iOS 27 has hidden new feature I’ve been loving

iOS 27 gave Apple Maps a handful of new features, and my favorite is one that keeps offering fresh updates every week: Local Lists.

Apple Maps has long offered a ‘Guides’ feature where you can browse curated collections of places worth checking out. Sometimes they’re created by Apple’s editorial team, other times by celebrities or in conjunction with current events.

But in iOS 27, there’s a new feature—Local Lists—that’s sort of an extension of Guides, but it gets updated weekly with the latest trending places.

Here’s how Apple describes it, via Apple Newsroom:

I’ve always enjoyed browsing Guides in Maps to help find new places. But Local Lists are a great expansion of the idea, especially since they’re updated all the time. I’m always up for trying a new trending restaurant, and now Maps makes it easy to stay on top of what’s new.

Even if you’ve been using iOS 27 for months, there’s a good chance you’ve never seen Local Lists. That’s because they’re pretty hidden.

To find the feature, tap into the search field in Maps and scroll down to see a new ‘Trending Restaurants’ section. On my iPhone 18 Pro, by default this section gets hidden behind the keyboard, so you have to first scroll and dismiss the keyboard to see it.

Trending Restaurants are ranked from 1-20. The search screen shows only a handful, but you can tap to view the full list. For example, if you open the ‘Trending Restaurants in New York’ list, you’ll see 20 places worth checking out.

How does a restaurant make the list? Per the in-app explanation, the list contains “Restaurants climbing in popularity this week, based on what people view, share, and interact with on Apple Maps.”

Since these Trending Restaurants lists update weekly, Apple says you’ll want to save any places you plan to visit. There’s a convenient + button next to each listing.

It’s unclear exactly how many different parts of the US have localized lists in iOS 27. But if you poke around and find the full collection of Local Lists, there are 1,021 total—so you’ll probably have one in your area.

You can browse all available lists by opening a Trending Restaurants list then tapping where you see the Apple logo and ‘Local Lists’ near the text that says when it was last updated.

Have you used Local Lists in iOS 27’s Maps app yet? Let us know what you think via the comments.

#3097. This tiny iOS 27 camera feature really makes a huge difference

When shooting both photos and videos on my iPhone, I make regular use of a few different third-party apps, mostly because I like to take manual control.

But a combination of the new Pro controls on the iPhone 18 Pro and a new feature introduced with iOS 27 means there are more times when I can stick to Apple’s stock Camera app. If you aren’t already using customizable controls, I highly recommend doing so …

Developers know that a big reason for using third-party camera apps is being able to use them in much the same way you would a standalone camera. A key part of this is having easy access to manual control over things like aperture (on the iPhone 18 Pro), shutter speed, white balance, and choosing between manual and auto focus. Those settings are right there on the main screen of almost all third-party apps.

With the iPhone 18 Pro, the same set of controls are also available in Apple’s stock camera app. By default, these are tucked inside a menu, requiring an initial tap to open it. As we noted back in September, however, iOS 27 brings customizable controls to the camera app.

Simply open the menu and tap the Edit button (top-left when holding the phone vertically) and you can add any of the controls to the main screen. This makes them available in a single tap.

Aperture, shutter speed, and white balance as these are the three main manual controls I use. Exposure compensation, because sometimes the only reason I want to take manual control is to increase or decrease the exposure, and that provides a faster way of doing so (quicker than the alternative drag up/down within the photo, in my experience). Finally, I have one-tap access to the histogram to help in setting exposure.

It’s a similar story in video mode. I again have aperture and white balance along with exposure compensation and the histogram. But here I add instant access to frame-rate and focus modes (as I’m more likely to switch focus mode when shooting video).

Of course, third-party apps still have an important role, but this one change has made a big difference to me when using the stock camera app for both photos and video.

Do you make use of this feature yourself? If so, please share the details in the comments.
